metadata.title: PSYC 305 Personality Psychology — Lectures 1–4 (Midterm 1)
metadata.subject: Personality Psychology
metadata.description: Practice for Midterm 1: defining personality and levels of analysis, person vs. situation, LOTS research methods, reliability and validity, open science, Freud and contemporary psychoanalytic approaches (repression, narcissism, attachment), motive theories, the humanistic perspective, the self and self-esteem.

objectives: Abu Ghraib; person vs. situation explanations of behavior
Self-Report, Observer report, Test data, Life history/ case study
Reliability of scales and observer report
Origins of theory (hysteria, Case of Anna O.)
Id, ego, superego; structure of the mind according to Freud
The cognitive unconscious vs. motivated unconscious
Ego psychology – Erikson’s stages of development
Know the basics of each theory

sections.title: Lecture 1 — What Is Personality?
sections.description: Everyday and scientific definitions of personality, the three levels of personality analysis, and what personality theories try to explain.

items.definition: In the scientific definition: consistent and enduring patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that influence a person's interactions with, and adaptations to, the environment.
items.source_excerpt: Consistent and enduring patterns of: thoughts, feelings, and behaviors… that influence a person’s interactions with, and adaptations to, the environment

items.question: Sam felt nervous once at a party last year but is relaxed in every other social setting. Why is that one episode weak evidence about Sam's personality?
options: Personality covers only behaviors, so a feeling of nervousness cannot count
Personality refers to consistent, enduring patterns rather than one occurrence
Feelings belong to the study of emotion, not to the study of personality
Only descriptive traits such as 'outgoing' count as parts of personality
items.explanation: The scientific definition requires consistent and enduring patterns of thoughts, feelings and behaviors; a single episode is not a pattern.
distractor_rationale: Feelings are explicitly part of the definition alongside thoughts and behaviors.
Emotions and emotional tendencies are listed as components of personality.
Traits are only one component; motives, values, emotions and life stories also count.
items.source_excerpt: Consistent and enduring patterns of: thoughts, feelings, and behaviors

items.question: A student says, "I expect most new classmates will turn out to be friendly." Which component of personality does this statement express?
items.explanation: Thoughts include beliefs, values and expectations; an expectation about others is a thought.
distractor_rationale: Behaviors are actions — what you do, like going to parties or being late.
Feelings are emotions and passions, such as feeling nervous on meeting someone.
Not one of the three components (thoughts, feelings, behaviors) of the definition.
items.source_excerpt: Thoughts (beliefs, values, expectations) – I think that relationships are more important than school

items.question: A friend is described as "honest and loyal." Which kind of personality characteristic does this description pick out?
items.explanation: Honest, loyal and selfish are given as examples of values, one of the characteristics that make up personality.
distractor_rationale: Motives and goals are things like being achievement- or relationship-motivated.
Emotional tendencies are things like moody, anxious or optimistic.
Traits are descriptive characteristics like intelligent or hard-working; honest and loyal are given as values.
items.source_excerpt: Values – honest, loyal, selfish • Emotional tendencies – moody, anxious, optimistic

items.front: Besides descriptive traits, what four other kinds of characteristics make up a personality?
items.back: Motives and goals; values; emotional tendencies; memories/life stories.
items.source_excerpt: Descriptive characteristics (i.e., traits) – intelligent, hard-working • Motives and goals – achievement-motivated, relationship-motivated • Values

items.definition: The Greek word meaning 'mask' — the character represented in a play — from which our word for personality comes.
items.source_excerpt: Greek word ‘persona’ (mask): character represented in a play

items.front: Why did actors in Ancient Greece wear masks, and what did the masks' expressions convey?
items.back: The actors (all men) wore masks so they could play multiple roles, including female parts; the facial expression conveyed the essence of the character, as well as sex, age and social class. That mask — the 'persona' — gives us the word personality.
items.source_excerpt: In Ancient Greece, the actors (all men) wore masks so that they could play multiple roles, including female parts.

items.question: When someone remarks that a person "has a lot of personality," which everyday sense of the word are they using?
items.explanation: 'She has a lot of personality' refers to social impact.
distractor_rationale: That is the sense in 'They have a rigid personality'.
That is the sense in 'He's got a good personality'.
Continuity is one of the uses illustrated by a complaint about a partner who never changes, not this phrase.
items.source_excerpt: ‘She has a lot of personality’ – social impact • ‘He’s got a good personality’ – social skills; likable

items.question: A coworker says: "He promises every year to stop interrupting people, and every year he keeps doing it." Which everyday use of personality does this illustrate?
items.explanation: Pointing to behavior that persists despite promises to change uses personality to express continuity, like 'Alex' complaining about his partner.
distractor_rationale: Evaluation is judging someone as good or likable, as when 'Jen' praises her date's personality.
Description lists what someone is like ('outgoing, friendly, kind of independent').
Social impact is the sense of 'she has a lot of personality'.
items.source_excerpt: I have told her a million times that I don’t like it, and she keeps saying she will change but never does.” • continuity

items.front: What three uses of 'personality' in everyday life are illustrated by a person praising a date, a person describing an old friend, and a person complaining about a partner?
items.back: Evaluation (praising the date), description (describing the friend), and continuity (the partner who never changes).
items.source_excerpt: it’s his personality that I like” • evaluation

items.front: What is the ultimate goal of personality psychology, and what do personality psychologists actually do to pursue it?
items.back: Understanding and explaining behavior. They carry out research, make assessments, and develop and test theories — across all aspects of the person and all contexts where personality is expressed.
items.source_excerpt: Personality psychologists carry out research, make assessments, and develop and test theories. • Ultimate goal is understanding and explaining behavior

items.question: A personality psychologist is hired by a test publishing company. What expertise are they most likely bringing?
options: Knowledge of what sells, and to whom
items.explanation: Test publishing companies employ personality psychologists for assessment expertise.
distractor_rationale: That is what they offer advertising and marketing firms.
That is what they offer organizational consulting firms.
Therapy is not among the workplaces or roles described for personality psychologists.
items.source_excerpt: Test publishing companies – Assessment expertise • Advertising/marketing – What sells, to whom

items.front: Complete Kluckhohn & Murray (1948): "Every person is in certain respects…"
items.back: …like all other people, like some other person, like no other person.
items.source_excerpt: “Every person is in certain respects: like all other people, like some other person, like no other person.” (Kluckhohn & Murray, 1948)

items.definition: The level of personality analysis concerned with how each person is 'like all others' — the universal ways in which all people are similar (e.g., we all need other people).
items.source_excerpt: …like all others = Human nature level (all people are similar in some ways; we all need other people)

items.definition: The level of personality analysis concerned with how each person is 'like some others' — people vary on common dimensions (e.g., some of us are more sociable than others).
items.source_excerpt: …like some others = Group level (people vary on common dimensions; e.g., some of us are more sociable than others)

items.definition: The level of personality analysis concerned with how each person is 'like no others' — what makes a single person's life unique.
items.source_excerpt: …like no others = Individual level (each person is unique)

items.question: "Albert discovered relativity" describes Albert at which level of personality analysis?
items.explanation: Discovering relativity is something only Albert did — it makes him 'like no others', the individual level.
distractor_rationale: Human nature would be something all people share, like enjoying a good meal.
The similar-sounding 'individual differences' (group) level is about common dimensions, like being good at math.
Not one of the three levels; situations are what social psychologists emphasize.
items.source_excerpt: …like no others = Individual level (each person is unique) -Albert discovered relativity

items.question: A theory proposes: "Extraverted people like to spend time with friends because they find it rewarding." What is this proposition about?
options: How and why people differ from each other
How situations make all people act alike
items.explanation: Contrasting extraverted people with others explains a difference between people, i.e., individual differences.
distractor_rationale: A human-nature claim applies to everyone, e.g., 'People need to feel included by others'.
A unique-case claim traces one person's life, like Margot's father's criticism at age 8.
That is the social-psychology focus on the power of the situation.
items.source_excerpt: How and why people differ from each other • “Men are more aggressive than women, because they have higher levels of Testosterone” • “Extraverted people like to spend time with friends because they find it rewarding.”

items.definition: Formal assumptions and propositions about human nature, about how and why people differ from each other, and about what makes an individual unique.
items.source_excerpt: Formal assumptions and propositions about: – Human nature • Universal aspects of personality

items.question: Someone cuts you off on the road; some drivers respond aggressively and others do not. Which level of analysis does this aggression example address?
items.explanation: In the same situation some people respond aggressively and others do not — a difference between people.
distractor_rationale: The human-nature case is that all people respond aggressively when their life is threatened and they cannot escape.
The unique case is an act understood only from one person's perspective, like Van Gogh cutting off his ear.
Fight-or-flight belongs to the universal (human nature) case, where everyone responds the same.
items.source_excerpt: In the same situation, some people respond aggressively whereas others do not – Someone cuts you off on the road.

items.front: Why is Vincent Van Gogh cutting off part of his ear and handing it to a woman at a brothel an example of the unique-case level of aggression?
items.back: Some acts of aggression can only be understood from the particular individual's perspective — they are not shared by all people or by a type of person.
items.source_excerpt: Some acts of aggression can only be understood from the particular individual’s perspective

items.front: What is the universal (human nature) case of aggression?
items.back: All people will respond aggressively if their life is being threatened and they cannot escape — the 'fight or flight' response.
items.source_excerpt: All people will respond aggressively if their life is being threatened and they cannot escape

items.question: Which statement correctly contrasts personality psychologists with social psychologists?
options: Social psychologists focus mostly on individual differences and on unique cases
Personality psychologists study only the human nature level of analysis
Personality researchers lean toward individual differences and the unique case
Both fields focus mainly on the unique case rather than on human nature
items.explanation: Personality researchers care about all three levels but focus more on individual differences and the unique case; social psychologists focus on the human-nature level.
distractor_rationale: This swaps the two fields' emphases.
Personality researchers care about all three levels, and lean away from human nature.
Social psychologists focus on how situations make ALL people behave in certain ways — human nature.
items.source_excerpt: But, we tend to focus more on individual differences and unique case • Social psychologists tend to focus on human nature level

items.front: What five themes in personality does The Royal Tenenbaums film excerpt illustrate?
items.back: Individual differences; motives, goals and emotions; personality change and continuity over time; childhood influences adulthood; how we can come to know a person.
items.source_excerpt: Individual differences • Motives, goals, and emotions • Personality change and continuity over time • Childhood influences adulthood

sections.title: Lecture 1 — Person vs. Situation: Stanford Prison, Abu Ghraib, and the Riots
sections.description: Applying the three levels of analysis to real events, and weighing 'rotten barrel' (situation) against 'rotten apples' (person) explanations of behavior.

items.front: Who ran the Stanford Prison Experiment, when, and what did participants do?
items.back: Philip Zimbardo, 1971. Stanford undergrads were recruited to play the role of prisoner or guard in a mock prison; they took their roles so seriously the study had to be shut down early.
items.source_excerpt: Stanford undergrads recruited to play the role of prisoner or guard in a mock prison – Participants took roles so seriously the study had to be shut down early!

items.question: In the Stanford Prison Experiment, 'guards' became sadistic and 'prisoners' became passive. What conclusion did Zimbardo draw?
options: The behavior showed the power of the situation
Only sadistic students volunteered as guards
The prisoners' passivity reflected compliant personalities
The experimenters had coached the guards' behavior
items.explanation: Zimbardo attributed the guards' cruelty and the prisoners' compliance to the power of the situation.
distractor_rationale: A person-based ('who were these participants?') explanation — raised as a critique, not Zimbardo's view.
A personality explanation; Zimbardo explained both roles by the situation.
Coaching is one of the critics' questions about the study, not Zimbardo's conclusion.
items.source_excerpt: “Guards” became sadistic and cruel • “Prisoners” became passive and compliant • Zimbardo: This is the power of the situation!

items.front: What three questions challenge Zimbardo's 'power of the situation' reading of the Stanford Prison Experiment?
items.back: How many guards actually became sadistic? Who were these participants? Was the behavior coached?
items.source_excerpt: But… how many guards became sadistic? Who were these participants? Was behavior coached?

items.definition: The situational explanation of abuse such as Abu Ghraib: the circumstances, not the people, caused it — e.g., 'Everyone would commit atrocities under these circumstances.'
items.source_excerpt: “Rotten barrel” (situation) • “Rotten apples” (people)

items.definition: The person-based explanation of abuse such as Abu Ghraib: the particular people involved, not the circumstances, caused it.
items.source_excerpt: “Rotten barrel” (situation) • “Rotten apples” (people)

items.question: Which observation counts against the 'rotten barrel' account of the Abu Ghraib abuse?
options: Humans have a sadistic impulse that will dominate
Stanford's prison study found the same
Virtually anybody in that situation would behave this way
items.explanation: If the situation were enough, everyone would have abused; that only 7 guards were sentenced (and only a few Stanford participants were abusive) points to the people involved. This supports the 'rotten apples' (people) account.
distractor_rationale: This is an argument for the situational (barrel) side.
Zimbardo cites his own study as support for the situational account.
This is Zimbardo's situational claim, not evidence against it.
items.source_excerpt: But, only 7 guards received prison sentences (and only a few of the participants in Zimbardo’s research were abusive)

items.question: Defenders of the guards said they were "probably loving husbands and fathers when they go on leave." Which point most directly challenges that claim?
options: Aggressive tendencies are generally stable over time and across situations
Humans have a sadistic impulse that will dominate in harsh circumstances like these
Anyone placed in that situation would have done the same thing
Wartime conditions unleash the dark side of human nature in everyone
items.explanation: If aggressive tendencies are stable across time and situations, someone abusive at the prison would not be expected to be gentle at home — as Graner's history of domestic violence shows.
distractor_rationale: This supports the situational account rather than challenging the 'loving husbands' claim.
This is Zimbardo's situational claim, which the 'loving husbands' argument supports.
A human-nature explanation; it is consistent with, not opposed to, the claim.
items.source_excerpt: Is this really true? Aggressive tendencies generally stable over time and across situations

items.front: What did Charles Graner's history before Abu Ghraib suggest about the cause of his abuse there?
items.back: A unique predisposition toward violence: multiple abuse allegations as a county prison guard and a history of domestic violence — he was not a 'loving husband' and seems unique in many ways.
items.source_excerpt: Graner’s personal history suggests a unique predisposition toward violence

items.question: A psychologist at her trial described Lynndie England as "an overly compliant personality in the face of perceived authority." At which level of analysis does this explanation operate?
items.explanation: Some people are more compliant to authority than others — a dimension people vary on, i.e., individual differences.
distractor_rationale: The unique-case explanation was applied to Graner's personal history of violence.
Human nature would say all people are capable of this, not that England is especially compliant.
A situational ('rotten barrel') account explains behavior by circumstances, not a personality trait.
items.source_excerpt: Some people are more compliant to authority than others

items.question: Which explanation of the Abu Ghraib abuse is pitched at the human nature level?
options: Some people are more inclined toward anti-social behavior
Graner's past shows a unique predisposition toward violence
All people are capable of evil in circumstances like these
Some people comply with perceived authority more than others
items.explanation: The human nature account holds that all people are capable of evil and the circumstances unleashed the dark side of human nature.
distractor_rationale: An individual-differences explanation — people vary in anti-social tendencies.
The unique-case explanation.
An individual-differences explanation applied to England.
items.source_excerpt: All people are capable of evil; the circumstances at Abu Ghraib unleashed the dark side of human nature

items.title: Explaining Abu Ghraib at three levels
items.context: Why did U.S. Army prison guards abuse prisoners at Abu Ghraib? Zimbardo said anyone would have done the same; President Bush said 'this is not American!'
steps: Human nature: all people are capable of evil; the circumstances unleashed the dark side of human nature (even the Dalai Lama might have felt a little hostile).

Individual differences: some people are more aggressive or inclined toward anti-social behavior than others, and some are more compliant to authority (England was called 'an overly compliant personality').
Unique case: Graner's personal history — abuse allegations as a prison guard and domestic violence — suggests a unique predisposition toward violence.
Weighing barrel vs apples: only 7 guards were sentenced, and aggressive tendencies are generally stable over time and across situations.
items.takeaway: One event can be explained at all three levels; personality researchers look especially at the individual-differences and unique-case explanations.
items.source_excerpt: Why did U.S. Army prison guards abuse the prisoners at Abu Ghraib? – Was it about human nature, individual differences, or unique case?

items.question: About 155,000 people were downtown during the 2011 Stanley Cup riot. If 10,000 of them contributed by cheering the rioters on, roughly what share of the crowd is that?
items.explanation: 10,000 / 155,000 ≈ 0.065, or about 6% — still a small minority, which points to personality rather than the situation alone.
distractor_rationale: 0.06% is the share actually arrested, not the share cheering.
A decimal-place slip: 10,000/155,000 is about 0.06, i.e., 6%, not 0.6%.
Reads the ratio as if most of the crowd took part.
items.source_excerpt: 155,000 people downtown – Only .06% arrested • unique cases – If 10,000 contributed to mayhem by cheering, that’s still only 6%

items.question: Which explanation of the Stanley Cup riot is an individual-differences explanation?
options: A desire to witness history in person
items.explanation: People differ in how excitement-seeking they are — a personality dimension, i.e., individual differences.
distractor_rationale: A situational (human nature) explanation affecting everyone downtown.
Situational/human nature — a motive anyone at the event could share.
Situational — a condition of the night, not a stable trait.
items.source_excerpt: Situation – Anger about the game, drunkeness, desire to witness history (human nature)

items.title: Person or situation? The 2011 Stanley Cup riot
items.context: On June 16th, 2011, rioting occurred throughout downtown Vancouver after the Canucks lost Game 7: break-ins, destruction of property, drunk and disorderly behavior; 268 suspects identified, 100 arrests, 'thousands' cheering.
steps: Situation (human nature): anger about the game, drunkenness, desire to witness history.
Personality: 155,000 people were downtown, but only .06% were arrested — those are unique cases.
Even if 10,000 contributed by cheering, that is still only about 6% of the crowd.
So individual differences — e.g., in excitement-seeking — help explain who took part.
items.takeaway: When only a small fraction of people in the same situation act a certain way, the situation alone cannot explain the behavior.
items.source_excerpt: On June 16th, 2011, rioting occurred throughout downtown Vancouver after the Canucks lost Game 7 of Stanley Cup

items.front: What claim did Zimbardo make about who would have committed the abuse at Abu Ghraib?
items.back: "You could put virtually anybody in that situation and you're going to get this kind of evil behavior" — the same thing he said his Stanford Prison Experiment found.
items.source_excerpt: “You could put virtually anybody in that situation and you’re going to get this kind of evil behavior.”

sections.title: Lectures 1–2 — Measuring Personality: Pre-Scientific and LOTS Methods
sections.description: Astrology, physiognomy and phrenology; the four LOTS descriptive methods (life history, observer report, test data, self-report), the TIPI, and choosing the right method.

items.question: A class picks which of 12 adjective sets best describes them, and each set secretly matches one star sign. What share of people would pick their own sign's set by chance alone?
items.explanation: With 12 sets, chance is 1 in 12 ≈ 8% — about 10 people in the class.
distractor_rationale: The chance rate for a four-option question, not twelve options.
Confuses the number of sets (12) with the percentage.
Far below 1-in-12; would require about 100 options.
items.source_excerpt: **8% (about 10 people) expected by chance

items.definition: A pre-scientific method of personality assessment based on a person's birth date.
items.source_excerpt: Astrology Ø Personality assessment based on birth date

items.definition: A pre-scientific method of personality assessment based on the shape of the body, particularly the face.
items.source_excerpt: Physiognomy Ø Personality assessment based on shape of body, particularly the face

items.definition: A pre-scientific method of personality assessment based on the morphology (shape) of the skull.
items.source_excerpt: Phrenology Ø Personality assessment based on morphology (shape) of skull

items.question: An 1800s assessor judges a man's character from the shape of his nose, jaw and face. Which pre-scientific method is this?
items.explanation: Physiognomy assesses personality from the shape of the body, particularly the face.
distractor_rationale: Phrenology reads the shape of the skull, not the face — the two are easily confused.
Astrology uses birth date, not physical features.
A modern test technique (e.g., the Rorschach), not a pre-scientific method.
items.source_excerpt: Physiognomy Ø Personality assessment based on shape of body, particularly the face Ø Phrenology

items.front: What do the letters of LOTS stand for in personality research?
items.back: The four major types of descriptive methods: Life history data, Observer-reports, Test data, Self-reports (surveys).
items.source_excerpt: There are 4 major types of descriptive methods Life History Data Observer-reports Test Data Self-reports (surveys) LOTS of data!

items.definition: Acronym for the four major types of descriptive methods in personality research: Life history data, Observer-reports, Test data, and Self-reports.
items.source_excerpt: There are 4 major types of descriptive methods Life History Data Observer-reports Test Data Self-reports (surveys) LOTS of data!

items.definition: A descriptive method that asks people questions about their beliefs and behaviors; the data are provided by the subject, e.g., as responses to questionnaires.
items.source_excerpt: Asking people questions about their beliefs and behaviors • Provided by the subject • Responses to questionnaires

items.definition: A brief self-report measure in which people rate how well each of ten pairs of traits applies to them on a 1–7 agree/disagree scale; each of five dimensions is scored by reverse-scoring one item and averaging it with its partner.
items.source_excerpt: Ten-Item Personality Inventory-(TIPI)

items.front: How is a TIPI dimension score calculated, using Extraversion as the example?
items.back: Reverse-score the negatively keyed item (#6 'Reserved, quiet': 1=7, 2=6, 3=5, 4=4, 5=3, 6=2, 7=1), then average it with the positively keyed item: E = (#6R + #1) / 2.
items.source_excerpt: Reverse your score on #6 [1=7, 2=6, 3=5, 4=4, 5=3, 6=2, 7=1] – (#6R + #1) divided by 2 = E score

items.question: On the TIPI, a student rates item #1 (Extraverted, enthusiastic) as 6 and item #6 (Reserved, quiet) as 2. What is their Extraversion score?
items.explanation: Reverse #6: 2 becomes 6. Then (6 + 6) / 2 = 6.0.
distractor_rationale: Forgets to reverse #6: (6 + 2) / 2 = 4.
Adds the reversed item and #1 but forgets to divide by 2.
Reverses the wrong item: #1 becomes 2, so (2 + 2) / 2 = 2.
items.source_excerpt: Reverse your score on #6 [1=7, 2=6, 3=5, 4=4, 5=3, 6=2, 7=1] – (#6R + #1) divided by 2 = E score

items.question: A student rates TIPI item #4 (Anxious, easily upset) as 5 and item #9 (Calm, emotionally stable) as 3. What is their Neuroticism score?
items.explanation: Reverse #9: 3 becomes 5. Then (5 + 5) / 2 = 5.0.
distractor_rationale: Reverses #4 instead of #9: (3 + 3) / 2 = 3.
Forgets to reverse #9: (5 + 3) / 2 = 4.
Sums the two items without dividing by 2.
items.source_excerpt: Neuroticism – Reverse your score on #9 – (#9R + #4) divided by 2 = N score

items.question: Which TIPI item must be reverse-scored when computing Conscientiousness?
items.explanation: Conscientiousness = (#8R + #3) / 2; 'Disorganized, careless' is the item keyed against conscientiousness.
distractor_rationale: #3 is the positively keyed Conscientiousness item and is not reversed.
#9 is reversed for Neuroticism.
#10 is reversed for Openness to Experience.
items.source_excerpt: Conscientiousness – Reverse your score on #8 – (#8R + #3) divided by 2 = C score

items.question: A student's TIPI Agreeableness score is 4.2. How does that compare with the average undergraduate (N = 2,249)?
items.explanation: The average undergraduate Agreeableness score is 5.09, so 4.2 is below average.
distractor_rationale: 4.16 is the average for Neuroticism, not Agreeableness.
4.55 is the average for Extraversion.
3.85 is undergraduates' mean Rosenberg self-esteem, not a TIPI average.
items.source_excerpt: Extraversion: 4.55 – Agreeableness: 5.09 – Conscientiousness: 4.82 – Neuroticism: 4.16 – Openness to experience: 4.87

items.front: Among average undergraduate TIPI scores, which dimension is highest and which is lowest?
items.back: Highest: Agreeableness (5.09). Lowest: Neuroticism (4.16).
items.source_excerpt: Agreeableness: 5.09 – Conscientiousness: 4.82 – Neuroticism: 4.16

items.definition: A personality dimension marked by being sociable, outgoing and talkative (TIPI pair: 'extraverted, enthusiastic' vs. 'reserved, quiet').
items.source_excerpt: Extraversion: sociable, outgoing, talkative

items.definition: A personality dimension marked by being friendly, nice and easy to get along with (TIPI pair: 'sympathetic, warm' vs. 'critical, quarrelsome').
items.source_excerpt: Agreeableness: friendly, nice, easy to get along with

items.definition: A personality dimension marked by being goal-oriented, hard-working and diligent (TIPI pair: 'dependable, self-disciplined' vs. 'disorganized, careless').
items.source_excerpt: Conscientiousness: goal-oriented, hardworking, diligent

items.definition: A personality dimension marked by being unhappy, anxious and stressed (TIPI pair: 'anxious, easily upset' vs. 'calm, emotionally stable').
items.source_excerpt: Neurotic: unhappy, anxious, stressed

items.definition: A personality dimension marked by being open-minded, creative and flexible (TIPI pair: 'open to new experiences, complex' vs. 'conventional, uncreative').
items.source_excerpt: Open to Experience: open-minded, creative, flexible

items.question: A manager describes an employee as unhappy, anxious and frequently stressed. On which dimension would observers rate this employee high?
items.explanation: Unhappy, anxious and stressed are the descriptors for the Neurotic dimension.
distractor_rationale: Agreeableness is friendly, nice and easy to get along with.
Openness is open-minded, creative and flexible.
Extraversion is sociable, outgoing and talkative.
items.source_excerpt: Neurotic: unhappy, anxious, stressed

items.question: Which is a recognized disadvantage of self-report data?
options: Responses may be biased or untruthful
Hard to distribute to large groups
items.explanation: Self-reports may be biased or untruthful, and respondents may not be representative (convenience sampling is tempting).
distractor_rationale: The opposite — self-reports are easy to distribute to large groups.
The opposite — self-report allows study of hard-to-observe thoughts and feelings.
Researcher interference is a disadvantage of observer data.
items.source_excerpt: Disadvantages – Respondents may not be representative (convenience sampling is tempting) – Responses may be biased or untruthful

items.question: A researcher wants to study private worries that rarely show in behavior, across 5,000 participants, on a small budget. Which method best fits?
items.explanation: Self-report allows study of difficult-to-observe thoughts and feelings and is easy to distribute to large groups.
distractor_rationale: Observers can't see private worries, and observation is time consuming.
A case study examines one person or group intensively and is hard to generalize.
Costly at this scale, and the researcher must infer what the test measures.
items.source_excerpt: Allows study of difficult-to-observe behaviors, thoughts and feelings • Who knows better? – Easy to distribute to large groups

items.definition: A descriptive method in which data come from observing the behavior of others — by parents, friends or teachers, trained observers, or untrained participant-observers.
items.source_excerpt: Descriptive Methods Observer Report Observing behavior of others

items.question: Students in a lecture rate two celebrities' personalities on a 1–5 scale. What kind of observers are they?
options: Close others using a rating form
items.explanation: Class ratings of Taylor and Oprah are the example of untrained participant-observers.
distractor_rationale: The students have no training and are not systematically coding behavior.
Parents, friends and teachers are close others; students don't know the celebrities.
They are rating other people, not themselves.
items.source_excerpt: Untrained, participant-observers – Class ratings of Taylor and Oprah

items.front: What are the two advantages of observer-report data, and its four disadvantages?
items.back: Advantages: captures spontaneous behaviors; avoids the bias of self-reports. Disadvantages: researcher interference (how naturalistic is it?); rarity of some behaviors; observer bias & selective attention; time consuming.
items.source_excerpt: Capture spontaneous behaviors – Avoid bias of self-reports • Disadvantages – Researcher interference

items.question: A researcher plans to study criminal behavior by directly observing people in public. Which limitation of observer data will most likely sink the plan?
options: Some behaviors are too rare to observe
Observers avoid the bias of self-reports
The test may not measure what it claims
items.explanation: Rarity of some behaviors is an observer-data disadvantage, with research on criminality as the example.
distractor_rationale: This is an advantage of observer data, not a limitation.
Untruthful responding is a self-report problem.
This validity worry is the disadvantage of test data.
items.source_excerpt: Rarity of some behaviors • Research on criminality

items.definition: Data from assessing an individual's abilities, cognitions, motivations or behaviors by observing their performance in a test situation, where the dependent variable is a score whose meaning the researcher assigned before the test.
items.source_excerpt: Assessing an individual’s abilities, cognitions, motivations, or behaviors, by observing their performance in a test situation

items.question: What is the critical element that makes a measurement count as test data?
options: It must be a written questionnaire with fixed items
The researcher fixes the score's meaning beforehand
It measures only abilities, not motives
items.explanation: The DV is a test score or result that has meaning only because the researcher assigned it that meaning before the test.
distractor_rationale: Tests may be written, physical (e.g., cardiogram), experimental or physiological.
Meaning comes from the researcher's prior assignment, not participants' interpretation.
Tests can assess abilities, cognitions, motivations or behaviors.
items.source_excerpt: The critical element of test data is that the DV is a test score or test result, which has meaning only because it was assigned that meaning by the researcher, prior to the test

items.question: A researcher records each person's startle reflex to a loud noise. When does this physiological measure count as test data?
options: Whenever any biological response is recorded
Only if the participant can explain their reaction
Only when trained observers code the response
When a theory links its strength to a diagnosis
items.explanation: It is test data if the researcher has a theory that a strong (or weak) startle response means some particular diagnosis.
distractor_rationale: Recording alone isn't enough; the response needs a meaning assigned in advance.
Test data can measure things not even known to the participant.
Coding by observers would make it observer data, which is not the defining feature here.
items.source_excerpt: This is test data if the researcher has a theory that a strong (or weak) startle response means some particular diagnosis

items.front: Name four kinds of test data and say where each gets its meaning or what it records.
items.back: Questionnaire tests (e.g., IQ) — meaning comes from the score, not participants' answers; experimental tests — meaning comes from performance; physiological — individual differences in biological responses (heart rate, startle, blood pressure); projective techniques (e.g., the Rorschach).
items.source_excerpt: Questionnaire tests – E.g., IQ – Meaning comes from score, not participants’ answers to questions

items.definition: A kind of test data, such as IQ, in which meaning comes from the score rather than from participants' answers to the questions.
items.source_excerpt: Questionnaire tests – E.g., IQ – Meaning comes from score, not participants’ answers to questions

items.definition: A kind of test data in which meaning comes from performance on a task, which indicates a particular result — e.g., who takes control in Megargee's box-repair task.
items.source_excerpt: Experimental tests Meaning comes from performance, which indicates a particular result

items.definition: Tests in which a person's perception of a stimulus (such as an inkblot) is taken to reveal something about their mental state or personality, interpreted with a codebook for what various responses mean.
items.source_excerpt: Perception of the stimulus reveals something about mental state or personality - Psychologists who use the Rorschach have a codebook for what various responses mean

items.question: In Megargee's (1969) box-repair task, a high-dominance woman was paired with a low-dominance man. Who usually took the leader role?
options: The woman, but only in 70% of pairs
items.explanation: Even when the woman was high and the man low in dominance, the man was still the leader (80%).
distractor_rationale: What trait dominance alone would predict — but gender won out in co-ed pairs.
The result was lopsided (80% the man), not an even or random split.
70% is the rate at which the high-dominance woman led in all-female pairs.
items.source_excerpt: High dom female, low dom male? • Male was still the leader! (80%)

items.front: In Megargee's same-sex pairs, who took the lead, and how often?
items.back: The high-dominance partner: 75% of male pairs and 70% of female pairs. (In co-ed pairs with a high-dominance man, the man led 90% of the time.)
items.source_excerpt: Male pairs? • High dom was leader (75%) – Female pairs? • High dom was leader (70%)

items.title: Megargee (1969): an experimental test of dominance and leadership
items.context: Does trait dominance (high vs. low) or gender predict leadership?
steps: Pair high- and low-dominance men and women in a 'box repair' task, forming 4 kinds of pairs.
DV = who takes control, which Megargee assumed indicates leadership — a meaning assigned before the test, making this test data.
Same-sex pairs: the high-dominance person led (male pairs 75%, female pairs 70%).
Co-ed, high-dominance man with low-dominance woman: the man led (90%).
Co-ed, high-dominance woman with low-dominance man: the man was STILL the leader (80%).
items.takeaway: Trait dominance predicted leadership within a gender, but in mixed pairs gender overrode it.
items.source_excerpt: Megargee (1969) study of dominance • Does trait dominance (high vs. low) or gender predict leadership?

items.question: A test claims to reveal motives that participants are not even aware of. What is the main weakness to worry about with this kind of measure?
options: It cannot reach things participants don't know about themselves
Whether it truly measures what it is thought to measure
Participants may answer in a socially desirable way
The findings cannot be generalized beyond N = 1
items.explanation: Test data can measure characteristics not even known to the participant, but you must infer the test measures what you think it measures — a validity issue.
distractor_rationale: The opposite — reaching characteristics unknown to the participant is test data's advantage.
Biased or untruthful responses are the classic self-report problem.
Generalizing from one case is the problem with case studies.
items.source_excerpt: Allows measurement of characteristics not easily observable, or even known to the participant • Disadvantages • Must infer that the test measures what you think it measures

items.definition: A descriptive method involving the intensive examination of a single person or group, drawing on life history (interviews, autobiography) and other life records.
items.source_excerpt: Descriptive Methods Case Studies (Life History) Intensive examination of a single person or group

items.definition: Life records used in case studies beyond interviews and autobiography — such as school grades, criminal records, work records, and social media posts.
items.source_excerpt: Other life records (Life Outcome Data) – School grades – Criminal records – Work record

items.question: A researcher writes an intensive analysis of a single serial offender's life. Which criticism applies most directly to this method?
options: Responses may be biased or untruthful
It is hard to generalize from N = 1
It cannot be used to study rare behaviors
The score's meaning must be set in advance
items.explanation: Case studies are difficult to generalize (N = 1), and are also open to observer bias and hard to reconstruct causes from past events.
distractor_rationale: The main self-report disadvantage.
The opposite — case studies allow the study of rare behaviors.
That describes what defines test data, not a case-study weakness.
items.source_excerpt: Disadvantages – Observer bias – Difficult to generalize (N = 1) – Difficult to reconstruct causes from complexity of past events

items.front: What are the two advantages of the case study method?
items.back: It is a rich source of hypotheses, and it allows the study of rare behaviors.
items.source_excerpt: Advantages – Rich source of hypotheses – Allows for studies of rare behaviors

items.question: Measuring shyness by whether a person walks in the middle or along the side of a hallway is classified as which kind of data?
items.explanation: Hallway walking is one of the behavioral test measures of shyness, alongside psychophysiology and brain imaging.
distractor_rationale: Life records include clubs joined, dates in the past year, or attending a reunion.
Observer measures of shyness are signs like shuffling feet, no eye contact, or a quivering voice.
Self-report is a questionnaire such as 'I find it difficult to talk to strangers.'
items.source_excerpt: Behavioral • Walking in the middle vs. side of hallway

items.question: A researcher counts how many social clubs a person has joined and how many dates they had in the past year. Which LOTS method is this?
items.explanation: Number of social clubs joined and dates in the past year are life records — life outcome data — for shyness.
distractor_rationale: Observation would involve watching behavior, like shuffling feet or perspiring.
Test measures for shyness include heart rate, cortisol and brain imaging.
Self-report would ask the person to rate items like 'I feel tense with strangers.'
items.source_excerpt: Life records data • # of social clubs joined • # of dates in the past year • Attended school reunion

items.title: Measuring shyness with LOTS of data
steps: Self-report: questionnaire items such as 'I feel tense when I'm with people I don't know well' and 'I find it difficult to talk to strangers.'
Observation: paces or shuffles feet, no eye contact, tense face muscles, moistens lips, clears throat, perspires, voice quivers.
Test: psychophysiology (heart rate, skin conductance, cortisol), brain imaging of responses to novel stimuli, and behavior (walking in the middle vs. side of a hallway).
Life records: number of social clubs joined, number of dates in the past year, whether the person attended a school reunion.
items.takeaway: One trait can be measured with all four LOTS methods, each with different strengths.
items.source_excerpt: “I feel tense when I’m with people I don’t know well.” “I find it difficult to talk to strangers.”

items.question: To understand Chuck Graner, a researcher collects ratings of him by his ex-spouse, other prison guards and his military supervisors. What type of data is this?
items.explanation: Ratings by people who know him are observer (O) data.
distractor_rationale: L-data would be life records like employment or court records.
S-data would be personality tests he completed himself on entering the military.
T-data would be IQ scores, brain imaging or physiological measures.
items.source_excerpt: O-data: Observer data – Ratings by Graner’s ex-spouse, other prison guards, military supervisor’s, his parents, etc.

items.front: Give one L, one T and one S data source that could be used to understand Chuck Graner.
items.back: L: employment records at the prison or court records on spousal abuse. T: IQ scores, brain imaging or other physiological measures. S: personality tests completed when he entered the military.
items.source_excerpt: L-data: Life records – Employment records at prison; court records related to spousal abuse

items.question: Observers rated strangers' personalities just from looking at their dorm rooms. For which set of traits were observers most accurate?
items.explanation: Observers were most accurate for Openness to Experience, Conscientiousness and Extraversion.
distractor_rationale: Includes two traits (agreeableness, neuroticism) not among the most accurately judged.
Only openness is correct here.
Swaps extraversion for neuroticism.
items.source_excerpt: Observers were most accurate in rating – Openness to Experience – Conscientiousness – Extraversion

items.front: In the dorm room study, how was the accuracy of observers' personality ratings determined?
items.back: By correlating observers' ratings with the occupant's self-ratings and with ratings by two close peers.
items.source_excerpt: (based on correlations with self ratings and ratings by two close peers)

items.front: Why can't one method be used for every trait? Give the example trait that observers judge easily.
items.back: Some traits are more easily judged by observers (e.g., extraversion), while other traits require a different method — such as looking at someone's dorm room.
items.source_excerpt: Some traits are more easily judged by observers – E.g., extraversion • Other traits require a different method

sections.title: Lecture 2 — Evaluating Measures: Reliability and Validity
sections.description: Three kinds of reliability, four kinds of validity, the bull's-eye analogy, and why validity depends on reliability (the height-judging example).

items.definition: The extent to which scores on a measure are stable and replicable, versus the amount of error or randomness in the measure.
items.source_excerpt: Extent to which scores on the measure are stable and replicable, vs. amount of error or randomness in the measure

items.definition: The degree to which a measure assesses what it is supposed to assess — in the bull's-eye analogy, whether you are actually hitting the bull's-eye.
items.source_excerpt: Degree to which measure assesses what it is supposed to assess

items.definition: Reliability judged by whether scores are highly correlated across two testing times.
items.source_excerpt: Test-retest reliability – Are scores highly correlated across two testing times?

items.definition: Reliability judged by how well the items on a single measure 'hang together' — whether all items measure the same construct, assessed by the correlation among the items.
items.source_excerpt: Internal consistency reliability – How do the items on a single measure “hang together”?

items.definition: Reliability judged by whether multiple observers agree; it applies to observer (O) data only.
items.source_excerpt: Inter-rater reliability – For O-Data only – Do multiple observers agree?

items.definition: Validity judged by whether a measure appears to measure what you think it measures — e.g., a shyness questionnaire whose items are obviously about shyness.
items.source_excerpt: Face validity – Does it measure what you think it measures? • E.g., shyness questionnaire

items.definition: Validity judged by whether a measure predicts an external criterion — e.g., whether shuffling feet predicts self-reported shyness.
items.source_excerpt: Predictive validity – Does it predict an external criterion? • Does shuffling predict self-reported shyness?

items.definition: Validity judged by a measure's relation to other measures of the same variable — e.g., self-report and observer report of a trait should be related.
items.source_excerpt: Convergent validity – Relation to other measures of same variable • Self-report and observer report should be related

items.definition: The overarching form of validity that encompasses face, predictive and convergent validity together.
items.source_excerpt: Construct validity – All of the above

items.question: A dart thrower's darts land in a tight cluster in the top-left corner of the board, far from the bull's-eye. In the bull's-eye analogy, what does this describe?
options: A measure that is valid but not reliable
A measure that is reliable but not valid
A measure that is both reliable and valid
A measure that is neither reliable nor valid
items.explanation: Reliability = hitting the same spot each time (the tight cluster); validity = actually hitting the bull's-eye (which they miss).
distractor_rationale: Reverses the analogy — consistency is reliability, being on target is validity.
They never hit the bull's-eye, so the measure is not valid.
The tight cluster shows they hit the same spot each time, so it is reliable.
items.source_excerpt: Reliability = are you hitting the same spot each time? ØValidity = are you actually hitting the bulls eye?

items.question: A phrenology device gives exactly the same skull reading every time the same person is measured. What can we conclude about it as a personality measure?
options: It is valid, because the readings are consistent
It is neither reliable nor valid as a measure
It is reliable, but that does not make it valid
It is valid but not reliable as a measure
items.explanation: Consistent readings make it reliable, but phrenology is the classic example of a measure that is reliable but not valid.
distractor_rationale: Confuses consistency (reliability) with measuring the right thing (validity).
Identical repeat readings show the device is reliable.
Backwards — its readings are consistent but don't capture personality.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: “Reliable but not Valid” — phrenology bust and apparatus

items.question: A researcher gives the same anxiety questionnaire to students in September and again in December, then correlates the two sets of scores. Which kind of reliability is being assessed?
items.explanation: Correlating scores across two testing times is test-retest reliability.
distractor_rationale: Inter-rater reliability asks whether multiple observers agree, for O-data only.
Internal consistency correlates items within one administration.
A type of validity — comparing different measures of the same variable — not reliability.
items.source_excerpt: Test-retest reliability – Are scores highly correlated across two testing times?

items.question: Before using a new 20-item shyness scale, a researcher checks whether every item correlates with the others. What is being checked?
options: Whether the scale has predictive validity
Whether multiple observers agree on scores
Whether scores stay stable across two testing times
Whether all items measure the same construct
items.explanation: Correlation among the items tells you whether they 'hang together' — internal consistency reliability.
distractor_rationale: Predictive validity requires an external criterion, not item correlations.
That is inter-rater reliability, which applies to observer data.
That is test-retest reliability, which needs two testing occasions.
items.source_excerpt: Do all items measure the same construct? – Correlation among the items

items.question: For which kind of data can inter-rater reliability be assessed?
items.explanation: Inter-rater reliability asks whether multiple observers agree, so it applies to O-data only.
distractor_rationale: A self-report has a single respondent, so there are no raters to compare.
Test scores have meaning assigned in advance; agreement between raters is an observer issue.
It is specifically restricted to O-data.
items.source_excerpt: Inter-rater reliability – For O-Data only – Do multiple observers agree?

items.question: Researchers test whether people's self-reported shyness scores relate to observers' ratings of the same people's shyness. Which kind of validity is this?
items.explanation: Relating a measure to other measures of the same variable (self-report vs. observer report) is convergent validity.
distractor_rationale: Face validity is whether a measure looks like it measures what you think.
Predictive validity uses an external criterion, like whether shuffling predicts self-reported shyness.
Inter-rater reliability compares observers with each other, not with self-report.
items.source_excerpt: Convergent validity – Relation to other measures of same variable • Self-report and observer report should be related

items.question: A researcher asks whether people who shuffle their feet in a lab task also report being shy on a questionnaire. Which kind of validity is the foot-shuffling measure being tested for?
items.explanation: 'Does shuffling predict self-reported shyness?' is the example of predictive validity — predicting an external criterion.
distractor_rationale: Face validity asks only whether it looks like a shyness measure, not what it predicts.
Internal consistency is about items within one measure hanging together.
Test-retest compares the same measure across two times.
items.source_excerpt: Predictive validity – Does it predict an external criterion? • Does shuffling predict self-reported shyness?

items.question: Which statement about the relationship between reliability and validity is correct?
options: Reliability can be high only if validity is high
A highly reliable measure is therefore valid
Validity can be high only if reliability is high
Reliability and validity are unrelated properties
items.explanation: Validity can only be high if reliability is high; more reliable measures provide a more valid assessment.
distractor_rationale: Reverses the dependency — a measure can be reliable but not valid.
Phrenology is reliable but not valid, so reliability is not enough.
They are linked: low reliability caps validity.
items.source_excerpt: Validity can only be high if reliability is high

items.question: Individual judges' guesses of a person's height correlated .71 to .86 with actual height, but the mean of 6 judges correlated .90. Why did averaging help?
options: Averaging makes the measure more reliable, and so more valid
Averaging removes the need for reliability in the first place
Single judges are always more valid than group averages
Six judges guarantee a perfect correlation with actual height
items.explanation: Combining judgments makes a measure more reliable, and more reliable measures provide a more valid assessment.
distractor_rationale: Averaging works precisely by raising reliability, which validity depends on.
The data show the opposite: the mean outperformed individual judges.
.90 is high but not perfect; combining improves rather than guarantees accuracy.
items.source_excerpt: Individual judges correlated .71 to .86 with actual height – Mean of 6 judges correlated .90 with actual height – If measures are more reliable, they provide a more valid assessment!

items.title: Inter-rater reliability and validity: judging height without a ruler
items.context: Observers estimate the instructor's height ('How tall am I?').
steps: Reliability: the average correlation between two judges is .76.
Combining judges raises reliability: the reliability of 5 judges is about .90.
Validity: individual judges correlate .71 to .86 with actual height.
The mean of 6 judges correlates .90 with actual height — higher than any single judge.
Principle: validity can only be high if reliability is high; more reliable measures give more valid assessments.
items.takeaway: Combining many judges (or many items on a personality test) yields fairly reliable and valid measures — reliabilities of about .80–.90.
items.source_excerpt: Average correlation between two judges = .76 – Reliability of 5 judges is about .90

items.front: How can personality researchers get fairly reliable and valid measures, and what reliabilities does this typically yield?
items.back: By combining the judgments of multiple people, or using multiple items on a personality test — giving reliabilities of about .80–.90.
items.source_excerpt: By combining the judgments of multiple people (or using multiple items on a personality test) we can get fairly reliable and valid measures of personality

items.question: A new 'leadership' scale gives nearly identical scores when people retake it a month later, but its scores predict nothing about who actually leads. How should it be evaluated?
options: Neither reliable nor valid in any sense
Both reliable and valid, since scores are stable
items.explanation: Stable scores across two times show test-retest reliability; failing to predict an external criterion means poor predictive validity.
distractor_rationale: Reverses the two: the stable retest scores are the reliability.
Stability across time is reliability, so it is not 'neither'.
Stability alone doesn't make a measure valid — it must measure what it is supposed to.
items.source_excerpt: Predictive validity – Does it predict an external criterion?

sections.title: Lecture 2 — Best Practices: QRPs, Power and Open Science
sections.description: Why incentives push researchers toward questionable research practices, what false-positive psychology showed, statistical power and sample size, and how open science and informed consumption of research help.

items.front: What is the incentive-structure problem in psychological science?
items.back: Published research is important for getting a job, tenure and grants and being viewed favorably, so scientists try to publish as much as they can — a balancing act with staying truthful that results in researchers taking shortcuts, and sometimes worse.
items.source_excerpt: Published research is important for getting a job, getting tenure, getting grants, and being viewed favorably in our field

items.front: Which two famous social psychologists were recently accused of data fraud?
items.back: Francesca Gino and Dan Ariely.
items.source_excerpt: two famous social psychologists, Francesca Gino and Dan Ariely, were accused of data fraud

items.definition: Decisions in design, analysis and reporting that increase the likelihood of achieving a positive result (and a positive response from editors and reviewers) — problematic, but not fraud.
items.source_excerpt: Decisions in design, analysis, and reporting that increase the likelihood of achieving a positive result

items.question: Which of these research decisions is a questionable research practice?
options: Posting the data in an online repository
Pre-registering the hypotheses before collecting any data
Running a large, adequately powered sample
Peeking at the data and adding DVs until one works
items.explanation: Peeking at data and collecting additional dependent variables are QRPs — choices that raise the chance of a positive result.
distractor_rationale: Sharing data is one of the recommended open-science practices.
Pre-registration is a remedy for QRPs, not one of them.
Adequate power is a feature of good research.
items.source_excerpt: QRPs: Using small samples, collecting additional dependent variables, peeking at data, dropping an experimental condition

items.question: A researcher tests whether the U.S. economy does better under Democrats. Getting no effect, they try counting different politicians, then measuring the economy excluding recessions, until one version is significant. What is this?
items.explanation: Trying analysis after analysis until you get the effect you want is a QRP: 'If you want to get a particular effect, keep trying...'
distractor_rationale: Pre-registration fixes the analysis in advance — the opposite of trying many versions.
It is the same researcher re-analyzing, not an independent lab.
No data were invented; flexible analysis is problematic without constituting fraud.
items.source_excerpt: QRP: If you want to get a particular effect, keep trying...

items.front: What did Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn (2011) show in 'False Positive Psychology' about flexible analysis decisions?
items.back: If enough possibilities are entertained, the likelihood of achieving a significant result could be over 80% — with enough QRPs they 'found' that listening to a Beatles song made people younger.
items.source_excerpt: If enough possibilities are entertained, the likelihood of achieving a significant result could be over 80%!

items.definition: The demonstration that decisions in analyses (small samples, extra DVs, peeking, dropping conditions) can push the chance of a significant result above 80% — enough to 'show' a Beatles song made people younger.
items.source_excerpt: False Positive Psychology • How do decisions in analyses affect the final results?

items.question: John, Loewenstein & Prelec (2012) surveyed 2,155 academic psychologists about 10 QRPs. What did they find?
options: Admission rates near zero, with each QRP seen as indefensible
Admissions up to 63%, and high ratings of each as defensible
About 80% admitted outright data fraud across the 10 practices
Up to 63% admission, but every QRP rated indefensible
items.explanation: Admission rates reached 63%, and each practice was rated highly 'defensible'.
distractor_rationale: The opposite of the finding on both counts.
80% is the false-positive figure from Simmons et al.; the survey was about QRPs, not fraud.
Gets the admission rate right but reverses the defensibility ratings.
items.source_excerpt: Up to 63% admission and high levels of each being “defensible”

items.front: What four things should researchers do to counter QRPs?
items.back: Increase disclosure in methods, results and hypotheses; pre-register hypotheses and studies (data collection rules, analytic strategies); share data; be a responsible scientist regardless of outcome.
items.source_excerpt: Increase disclosure in methods, results, and hypothesis presentation • Pre-register hypotheses and studies

items.definition: Posting a study's hypotheses, data collection plans and analytic strategies in an online repository before the study is run.
items.source_excerpt: Data collection plans, analyses, and hypotheses are “pre-registered” and posted in an online repository

items.question: Why would pre-registering a study's analytic strategy make the 'keep trying until it works' problem harder to commit?
options: It guarantees that the sample will be large enough
It commits the analysis plan before data exist
It makes all the materials and data public
It ensures that other labs will replicate it
items.explanation: Pre-registration fixes data collection rules and analytic strategies in advance, so flexible analysis choices can't be made after seeing the data.
distractor_rationale: Sample size is about power — a separate feature of good research.
That is data sharing, a different open-science practice.
Replication by other labs is a separate check a consumer should look for.
items.source_excerpt: Pre-register hypotheses and studies – Data collection rules, analytic strategies

items.definition: An open-source software platform, from the Center for Open Science, for pre-registering hypotheses, archiving study materials, and depositing data and syntax.
items.source_excerpt: Open-source software platform for pre-registering hypotheses, archiving study materials, depositing data and syntax

items.front: Who founded the Center for Open Science, and why?
items.back: Brian Nosek and Jeff Spies — to increase the openness, integrity and reproducibility of scientific research. It runs the Open Science Framework, a platform for pre-registering hypotheses and depositing data and syntax.
items.source_excerpt: Founded to increase to openness, integrity, and reproducibility of scientific research – Brian Nosek and Jeff Spies

items.front: What four features mark 'good research' in the open-science sense?
items.back: It is open (materials and data shared publicly); its experimental methods are strong and isolate a question of interest; it is adequately 'powered'; and its data collection plans, analyses and hypotheses are pre-registered in an online repository.
items.source_excerpt: Good research is open research – Materials and data are shared publicly

items.definition: Research practice in which materials and data are shared publicly, with the goal of increasing the openness, integrity and reproducibility of scientific research.
items.source_excerpt: Good research is open research – Materials and data are shared publicly

items.definition: The chance of finding an effect that exists; generally set at 80%. Small effects require large samples to achieve it.
items.source_excerpt: Generally set at 80% – This means there’s an 80% chance of finding an effect that exists

items.question: Which study needs the larger sample to be adequately powered?
options: Comparing how liberal UBC students and Texan oil tycoons are
Comparing average height between men and women
Comparing how liberal UBC students and SFU students are
Any of these — power doesn't depend on effect size
items.explanation: UBC vs. SFU students is likely a small effect, and small effects need big samples; the other comparisons involve big effects.
distractor_rationale: A likely big effect, for which a smaller sample is fine.
The height difference is large; 12 people total suffices.
Needed sample size depends on whether the effect is likely small or big.
items.source_excerpt: If you’re studying an effect that’s likely to be small, you need a big sample • E.g., Are UBC or SFU students more liberal?

items.question: Detecting the gender difference in height takes about 12 people in total, but detecting the gender difference in weight takes about 92. What does this imply?
options: Weight is measured less reliably than height
Power for the weight study is set at 92%
The weight difference is the smaller effect
Weight studies must sample far more women
items.explanation: Smaller effects need bigger samples, so needing 92 rather than 12 participants indicates the weight difference is the smaller effect.
distractor_rationale: Nothing in the example concerns measurement error; it illustrates effect size and sample size.
Confuses the required sample (92) with the power level, which is conventionally 80%.
The figures are total sample sizes, not a requirement about one gender.
items.source_excerpt: Average Weight: – 170 lbs vs. 152 lbs (in Canada) • Required sample size? – 92 (total)

items.front: Why were studies before this decade often run with much lower power than 80%?
items.back: Researchers underestimate how much data are needed; effects are smaller than they think; and it's hard and expensive to collect large samples.
items.source_excerpt: Researchers underestimate how much data are needed • Effects are smaller than they think • It’s hard and expensive to collect large samples

items.front: Why do most psychology studies need a lot of participants, and what rough number do some researchers suggest?
items.back: Most psychological effects are small; some say 'around 200' participants, while others say it depends on what you're studying and your design.
items.source_excerpt: Most psychological effects are small, so you need a lot of participants – Some say “around 200”

items.question: Two studies report the same surprising effect. All else equal, which should an informed consumer of science trust more?
options: A 50-person study run once, with data kept private
A 50-person study whose effect seems almost unbelievable
