items.explanation: Traumatic events are often not repressed: many can't be forgotten (e.g., PTSD in veterans), and most victims recall the events 10–15 years later.
distractor_rationale: Improvement after recovery is cited in support of recovered memories, not against repression.
This is the recovered-memory therapists' claim.
Describes the aim of a therapy, not evidence about whether trauma is repressed.
items.source_excerpt: Studies show that most victims of incest and childhood abuse typically recall these events 10-15 years later

items.question: Post-traumatic stress disorder in veterans is used as evidence about repression. What does it show?
options: That trauma is usually pushed out of awareness
That many traumatic events can't be forgotten
That recovered memories are usually accurate
That trauma affects only the body, not the mind
items.explanation: PTSD illustrates that many traumatic events can't be forgotten — the opposite of repression.
distractor_rationale: The reverse — PTSD shows trauma stays in awareness.
PTSD speaks to whether trauma is forgotten, not to the accuracy of recovered memories.
PTSD is not raised as a body-only phenomenon.
items.source_excerpt: In fact, many can’t be forgotten – Post-traumatic stress disorder in veterans

items.question: Of 2,524 adults, 46% had experienced psychotherapy, and 20% of those said their therapist suggested possible repressed memories of abuse. Roughly what share of the whole sample is that?
items.explanation: 0.46 × 0.20 ≈ 0.09, so about 9% of the total sample.
distractor_rationale: 20% is the share of therapy-goers, not of the whole sample.
5% of the total is the share who recalled memories of abuse through therapy.
46% is the share who had any psychotherapy.
items.source_excerpt: Recruited 2,524 adults – 46% reported experiences of psychotherapy – Of those… • 20% (9% of total sample) said that therapist had suggested possible repressed memories of abuse

items.front: In the survey of 2,524 adults, what share recalled abuse memories through therapy, and what happened to many of them?
items.back: 11% of therapy-goers (5% of the total) recalled memories of abuse through therapy; of those, 43% became estranged from their family.
items.source_excerpt: 11% (5% of total) recalled memories of abuse through therapy – Of those, 43% became estranged from family

items.front: What evidence is offered on the other side — that recovering repressed memories can help?
items.back: Many patients and clinicians report major mental health improvements after recovered memories (e.g., Tim Ferriss recovered abuse memories during an ayahuasca ceremony); psychedelic therapy often aims to uncover repressed memories, and there is evidence it is effective for depression and PTSD.
items.source_excerpt: Many patients and clinicians report major mental health improvements following recovered memories

items.question: Which statement best summarizes the current conclusion about repressed memories?
options: Recovered memories are always false and should be ignored
Recovery is hard to verify, though many report improvement
Traumatic memories are usually repressed and later recovered
Recovered memories are reliable enough to support convictions
items.explanation: It is very difficult to prove whether a recovered memory is true and memories of mundane events can be implanted — yet many people report improved mental health after recovering memories.
distractor_rationale: Too strong — the evidence shows memories can be implanted, not that all recovered memories are false.
Most victims recall trauma years later; trauma is often not repressed.
The Franklin conviction was overturned for exactly this unreliability.
items.source_excerpt: Very difficult to prove whether a recovered memory is true • It is possible to implant memories of mundane events

items.definition: The view that we bury hidden needs and desires in the unconscious.
items.source_excerpt: Motivated view: We bury hidden needs/desires in the unconscious

items.definition: The view that information we perceive may become unconscious and influence us, without being 'buried' there by desire — similar to Freud's preconscious.
items.source_excerpt: Cognitive view: information perceived may become unconscious and influence us, but it’s not “buried” there

items.question: A brand logo flashed too quickly to notice later nudges your choices. Which view of the unconscious handles this without positing hidden desires?
options: The motivated view of the unconscious
The cognitive view of the unconscious
items.explanation: The cognitive view holds that perceived information can become unconscious and influence us without being 'buried' there by desire.
distractor_rationale: The motivated view says we bury hidden needs and desires — the opposite emphasis.
Jung's concept is about shared ancestral images, not recently perceived information.
Freud's unconscious is full of repressed desires — a motivated view.
items.source_excerpt: There is an unconscious, but does it really have “desires”?

items.definition: Presenting concepts in a way that lets them be perceived and influence us without our even knowing it.
items.source_excerpt: Subliminal Priming – Concepts may be perceived and influence us, without our even knowing it

items.question: In the Lipton Ice Tea study, a participant who is NOT thirsty is subliminally primed with the tea brand. What does the study predict?
options: A strong preference for the tea
No increased preference for buying the tea
A preference for whatever drink is placed first
An aversion to the tea because of the priming
items.explanation: Primed participants were more likely to buy the tea — but only if they were thirsty to begin with.
distractor_rationale: That happened only among participants who were already thirsty.
Nothing suggests position effects; the effect was specific to the primed tea.
No reverse effect is reported; the effect simply depends on thirst.
items.source_excerpt: Participants more likely to buy tea over other drink • But, only if thirsty to begin with

items.question: Why is product placement in a film the most effective form of priming?
options: Viewers consciously notice and remember the brand
Absorbed viewers lack the resources to resist it
It works only on people already thirsty for it
The product is shown too briefly to be perceived
items.explanation: When the placement is subtle, the observer is engrossed in the film/TV and can't use cognitive resources to prevent the ad's impact.
distractor_rationale: The point is the opposite — it works because it isn't consciously processed and resisted.
That is the Lipton finding's condition for subliminal priming, not why placement works.
Placements are embedded and visible; the issue is attention, not exposure time.
items.source_excerpt: If it’s subtle, observer is engrossed in film/TV, so can’t use cognitive resources to prevent the impact of the ad

items.front: What is controversial about subliminal priming?
items.back: It's not clear that subliminal priming of concepts actually influences BEHAVIOR.
items.source_excerpt: But, it’s not clear that subliminal priming of concepts actually influences BEHAVIOR

items.definition: The approach of Freud's students Anna Freud and Erik Erikson: a more complex view of the ego focused on the strengths of the conscious self and control over one's environment, whose goal is a secure identity — the beginning of research on the Self.
items.source_excerpt: Anna Freud, Erik Erikson – Students of Freud • More complex view of ego • Focus on the strengths of conscious self

items.definition: In ego psychology, what results from failing to establish a secure identity.
items.source_excerpt: Goal is to establish a secure identity – Failure to do so creates identity crisis

items.question: In ego psychology, what results when a young adult fails to establish a secure identity?
items.explanation: Ego psychology's goal is a secure identity; failure to establish one creates an identity crisis.
distractor_rationale: Repression pushes traumatic memories out of awareness; it isn't the outcome of failed identity.
A narcissistic wound is an early humiliation experience linked to narcissism.
Separation anxiety is a child's distress until mother returns.
items.source_excerpt: Goal is to establish a secure identity – Failure to do so creates identity crisis

items.definition: What follows when the conflict that marks a developmental stage is not resolved — called a 'crisis' in Erikson's words.
items.source_excerpt: Failure to resolve conflict leads to fixation, or crisis (in Erikson’s words)

items.question: How do Erikson's 8 stages of development differ from Freud's psychosexual stages?
options: Erikson's stages are free of conflict
They span the full lifespan, adulthood too
Failing a stage carries no lasting cost
They end at puberty, just as Freud's stages do
items.explanation: Erikson's stages cover the full lifespan, including ages 6–puberty (Freud's 'latency' period) and adulthood.
distractor_rationale: Like Freud's, each Erikson stage is marked by conflict.
Like Freud's, failure to resolve the conflict leads to fixation, or 'crisis'.
The reverse — Erikson extends development through adulthood.
items.source_excerpt: Different from Freud’s psychosexual development – Cover the full lifespan – Allow for development ages 6-puberty

items.front: In what two ways are Erikson's stages similar to Freud's?
items.back: Each stage is marked by conflict, and failure to resolve the conflict leads to fixation (or 'crisis', in Erikson's words).
items.source_excerpt: Similar to Freud’s – Each stage marked by conflict – Failure to resolve conflict leads to fixation

sections.title: Lecture 3 — Narcissism
sections.description: Narcissism as a Freudian defense: the narcissistic paradox, causes, measurement, normal-range findings, the self-enhancement video study, and grandiose vs. fragile narcissism.

items.definition: Exaggerated positive self-esteem; in normal (non-clinical) populations it shows up as self-enhancement — bragging, egotism, superiority, derogation of others, entitlement.
items.source_excerpt: Narcissism • Exaggerated positive self-esteem

items.definition: The observation that people who seem to think they're great may feel insecure underneath.
items.source_excerpt: Narcissistic Paradox: People who seem to think they’re great may feel insecure underneath

items.question: A coworker constantly brags about how brilliant he is, yet in therapy he turns out to feel deeply insecure. Which concept names this mismatch?
items.explanation: The narcissistic paradox: people who seem to think they're great may feel insecure underneath.
distractor_rationale: Self-enhancement bias measures how far self-ratings exceed objective ones, not hidden insecurity.
A narcissistic wound is the early humiliation thought to cause narcissism, not the present mismatch.
Grandiose narcissists have little insight, but the term doesn't name the outward/inner contrast.
items.source_excerpt: Narcissistic Paradox: People who seem to think they’re great may feel insecure underneath

items.question: If narcissists feel insecure underneath but display grandiose self-views, which defense mechanism is narcissism best seen as?
items.explanation: Narcissism is a defense — reaction formation: displaying the exact opposite (grandiosity) of an unacceptable feeling (insecurity).
distractor_rationale: Projection sees one's own unacceptable qualities in others; the key here is displaying the opposite.
Displacement redirects an impulse to another target, not into its opposite.
Rationalization supplies acceptable logical reasons; it doesn't flip insecurity into its opposite.
items.source_excerpt: Narcissism is a defense • Reaction formation

items.question: How does narcissism in normal (non-clinical) populations differ from the DSM characterization?
options: It is characterized mainly by self-enhancement
The DSM lists self-enhancement only, not dominance
items.explanation: The DSM lists grandiosity, dominance, entitlement and superiority; in normal populations narcissism is characterized by self-enhancement — an excessively positive view of self and negative view of others.
distractor_rationale: Narcissism is exaggerated positive self-esteem.
The DSM characteristics are grandiosity, dominance, entitlement and superiority.
Self-enhancement involves comparing: positive view of self, negative view of others.
items.source_excerpt: DSM characteristics: grandiosity, dominance, entitlement, superiority • In normal (non-clinical) populations, characterized by self-enhancement

items.definition: An excessively positive view of self and negative view of others — bragging, egotism, superiority, derogation of others and entitlement; the hallmark of narcissism in normal populations.
items.source_excerpt: i.e., excessively positive view of self and negative view of others

items.front: What did Armand Hammer do that made him a 'classic narcissist' example?
items.back: He bought Leonardo da Vinci's 'Codex Leicester' and renamed it 'Codex Hammer' (and said his mind's brilliance 'can only be described as dazzling'). After his death, Bill Gates bought it and renamed it back.
items.source_excerpt: Bought Leonardo DaVinci’s book “Codex Leicester” and renamed it “Codex Hammer”

items.question: Which parenting pattern is proposed as a cause of narcissism?
options: Consistent warmth with realistic expectations of the child
Over-idealizing the child yet harshly criticizing failure
Neglecting the child and setting no standards at all
Praising effort while ignoring both success and failure
items.explanation: Parents over-idealize the child and set unrealistic standards, while also excessively criticizing the child for failing to meet them. A 'narcissistic wound' — an early humiliation experience — is also implicated.
distractor_rationale: Realistic standards are the opposite of the unrealistic ones described.
The described parents are highly involved, setting very high standards.
The described pattern focuses on unmet standards and criticism, not ignoring outcomes.
items.source_excerpt: Parents over-idealize child, set up unrealistic standards • Simultaneously, parents excessively criticize child for failing to meet unrealistic standards

items.definition: An early humiliation experience thought to contribute to narcissism, for which the person later overcompensates by self-aggrandizing.
items.source_excerpt: “Narcissistic wound” – early humiliation experience • Narcissists overcompensate for insecurities by self-aggrandizing

items.question: The narcissism item "I will never be satisfied until I get all that I deserve" taps which facet?
items.explanation: That item measures a strong sense of entitlement (26% agree).
distractor_rationale: Self-importance is tapped by 'I am an extraordinary person.'
Fantasies are tapped by 'If I ruled the world it would be a much better place.'
Unrealistic beliefs about abilities: 'I can make anybody believe anything I want them to.'
items.source_excerpt: Strong sense of entitlement – “I will never be satisfied until I get all that I deserve.” – 26% agree

items.question: Agreeing with "If I ruled the world it would be a much better place" indicates which narcissistic characteristic?
items.explanation: Being preoccupied with fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance and beauty is tapped by this item (45% agree).
distractor_rationale: Entitlement is 'I will never be satisfied until I get all that I deserve.'
Self-importance is 'I am an extraordinary person.'
Abilities is 'I can make anybody believe anything I want them to.'
items.source_excerpt: Preoccupied with fantasies of unlimited success, power, brilliance, and beauty – “If I ruled the world it would be a much better place.” – 45% agree

items.front: What share of people agree with the narcissism item "I am an extraordinary person," and which characteristic does it measure?
items.back: 55% agree — it measures a grandiose sense of self-importance.
items.source_excerpt: Grandiose sense of self-importance – “I am an extraordinary person.” – 55% agree

items.question: Why do narcissists typically end up in therapy?
options: To work on their low self-esteem directly
For external life problems in work and love
Because they recognize their own entitlement
To recover repressed memories of childhood
items.explanation: Narcissists typically go to therapy for external life problems: work (repeated failures, unmet career expectations) and love (idealizing and devaluing partners, needing to be the center of attention).
distractor_rationale: They come for external problems, not to address self-esteem.
Grandiose narcissists have little psychological insight into their own motives.
Recovered memories belong to the repression debate, not narcissism.
items.source_excerpt: Narcissists typically go to therapy for external life problems – Work

items.front: A clinician expects quick progress treating a client with Narcissistic Personality Disorder. Is that expectation realistic?
items.back: No — NPD is very difficult to treat in therapy.
items.source_excerpt: Narcissistic Personality Disorder is very difficult to treat in therapy

items.question: A person high in normal-range narcissism gets harsh negative feedback on a group project they led. How are they most likely to respond?
options: With anger, blaming the others for the failure
With humility, taking full blame for the failure
With indifference, as feedback doesn't matter to them
items.explanation: Narcissists take credit for accomplishments but blame others for failures, and respond with anger and aggression to failure or negative feedback.
distractor_rationale: The opposite — they blame others for failures.
They react strongly — with anger and aggression — to negative feedback.
Their response to failure is anger and aggression, not withdrawal.
items.source_excerpt: Take credit for accomplishments but blame others for failures

items.front: List five research findings on normal-range narcissism.
items.back: Narcissists look in the mirror more often; take credit for successes but blame others for failures; self-promote more on social-networking sites; adopt a 'game-playing' style in relationships; become angry and aggressive after failure or negative feedback.
items.source_excerpt: Narcissists look in the mirror more frequently • Take credit for accomplishments but blame others for failures

items.definition: The degree to which a person's self-evaluation is more positive than an objective evaluation of their performance.
items.source_excerpt: DV: Self-Enhancement Bias = degree to which selfevaluation is more positive than objective evaluation

items.title: How deep-seated are narcissistic illusions? The videotape study
items.context: Would narcissists still self-enhance if they could see themselves through others' eyes?
steps: Self-evaluation: participants rate their own performance relative to other group members.
Objective evaluation: ratings from 12 psychologists, the 5 other group members ('peers'), and the objective task outcome (success vs. failure).
DV: self-enhancement bias — how much more positive the self-evaluation is than the objective one.
IV: self-focused attention. Control = evaluate immediately after the group discussion; Self-focused = evaluate after watching a videotape of oneself in the discussion.
Result: after the video, narcissists rated themselves even MORE positively, while non-narcissists' ratings moved toward their objective performance.
Comments: a narcissist 'liked watching myself very much'; a non-narcissist found it 'quite a sobering experience.'
items.takeaway: Seeing themselves as others do did not make narcissists less grandiose — their illusions are deep-seated.
items.source_excerpt: Experiment: Manipulated visual perspective via video – Show narcissists how others see them

items.question: After watching a videotape of themselves in a group discussion, how did narcissists' self-evaluations change compared with the control condition?
options: They stayed exactly the same as before
items.explanation: Narcissists' self-perceived performance rose further in the self-focused condition, while non-narcissists moved toward objective performance ('quite a sobering experience').
distractor_rationale: That describes non-narcissists, who found the video sobering.
Their ratings shifted, rising rather than staying flat.
Nobody fell below objective performance; narcissists moved further above it.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: “How will people rate their performance in each condition?” — Narcissists, Non-Narcissists, Objective Performance; Control vs. Self-Focused

items.question: In the narcissism videotape study, what was the independent variable?
options: Ratings by 12 psychologists and by 5 peers
Success or failure on the group task
Viewing a video of oneself before rating
items.explanation: The IV was self-focused attention, manipulated by having participants evaluate their performance after viewing a videotape of themselves (vs. immediately).
distractor_rationale: These ratings formed the objective evaluation used to compute the DV.
Self-enhancement bias was the dependent variable.
Task outcome was one source of the objective evaluation, not a manipulation.
items.source_excerpt: IV: Manipulation of Self-Focused Attention – Control Condition: • Evaluate performance immediately after group discussion

items.definition: A pathological narcissist with an exaggerated sense of self-importance who appears privileged and entitled, has little empathy, blames failures on others or circumstances, is critical and controlling, and has little psychological insight into their own motives.
items.source_excerpt: Grandiose narcissist • Has an exaggerated sense of self-importance • Appears to feel privileged and entitled • Has little empathy

items.definition: A pathological narcissist who tends to feel unhappy, depressed, anxious and envious, is prone to painful feelings of emptiness and of being inadequate or a failure — yet also has an exaggerated sense of self-importance, feels entitled and is critical of others.
items.source_excerpt: Fragile narcissist • Tends to feel unhappy, depressed, or despondent • Tends to be critical of others

items.question: Which characteristic is shared by BOTH grandiose and fragile narcissists?
options: Prone to painful feelings of emptiness
Tends to be critical of others
Tends to be controlling of others
items.explanation: Both profiles tend to be critical of others (and both have an exaggerated sense of self-importance and feel privileged and entitled).
distractor_rationale: Listed only for the fragile narcissist.
Listed only for the grandiose narcissist.
Listed only for the grandiose narcissist.
items.source_excerpt: Tends to be critical of others • Tends to be controlling • Has little psychological insight into own motives, behavior, etc.

items.question: A 40-year-old patient presents as vulnerable, depressed and low in self-esteem, yet resents daily responsibilities as a 'hassle' he shouldn't have to do and can't tolerate accommodating others' schedules. What covert presentation does this suggest?
items.explanation: The overt presentation is vulnerable/low self-esteem, but the entitlement and resentment underneath point to a covert presentation of fragile narcissism.
distractor_rationale: Nothing about his isolation and resentment fits a secure style.
A grandiose narcissist wouldn't overtly present as vulnerable with low self-esteem.
An attachment style, not the covert narcissistic presentation the entitlement points to.
items.source_excerpt: Overt Presentation: Vulnerable, Low Self-Esteem

items.title: A real clinical case: fragile narcissism beneath vulnerability
steps: Overt picture: 40-year-old college-educated single man, socially isolated, 'empty' depression, anhedonia, self-critical, chronically suicidal; ECT and medication did not help; pursuing disability; living with parents.
Overt presentation: vulnerable, low self-esteem.

More information: won't play guitar because no one pays to hear him; feels daily responsibilities are a 'hassle' he shouldn't have to do; lived off a depleted trust fund; resents parents for aging and having fewer resources; can't hold a job because he resents accommodating others' schedules; can't tolerate 'other people's crap'; everything becomes 'flawed'; withheld information in treatment.
Covert presentation: fragile narcissism?
items.takeaway: Entitlement and resentment can sit beneath an overtly vulnerable, low-self-esteem presentation — the fragile narcissist profile.
items.source_excerpt: Feels that daily responsibilities are a “hassle” and he should not have to do them

sections.title: Lectures 3–4 — Object Relations Theory and Attachment
sections.description: From Harlow's monkeys, Bowlby and Ainsworth's Strange Situation to Hazan & Shaver's adult attachment styles, the stress-test and memory studies, and whether attachment changes across the lifespan.

items.definition: A contemporary psychoanalytic approach emphasizing social relationships: adult relationships originate in childhood, and internalized (i.e., unconscious) representations of parents become the basis for relating to others.
items.source_excerpt: Internalized (i.e., unconscious) representations of parents become basis for relating to others

items.title: Harlow (1958): wire mother vs. cloth mother
steps: Infant monkeys were raised apart from their mothers.
They were given a surrogate 'wire' mom or a surrogate 'cloth' mom; the wire mom provided food and water.
Question: which surrogate would the monkeys spend most time with?
Result: even when the wire mom provided food, infant monkeys stayed close to the cloth mom.
Monkeys deprived of real mothers became anxious and insecure and showed abnormal sexuality.
items.takeaway: Physical contact between infant and caregiver matters — not just being fed.
items.source_excerpt: Raised monkeys apart from mother • Provided surrogate “wire” mom or surrogate “cloth mom” • Surrogate wire mom provided food and water

items.question: Infant monkeys stayed close to a cloth surrogate even when only a wire surrogate provided food. What does this show?
options: Infants attach to whoever provides food
Physical contact with a caregiver matters
Monkeys prefer any caregiver to none
Wire surrogates produced secure, calm infants
items.explanation: The result shows the importance of physical contact between infant and caregiver.
distractor_rationale: The opposite — they chose the cloth mom even though the wire mom fed them.
Doesn't explain why they preferred the cloth mom over the wire mom.
Monkeys deprived of real mothers became anxious and insecure.
items.source_excerpt: Even when wire mom provided food, infant monkeys stayed close to cloth mom Importance of physical contact between infant and caregiver.

items.front: If an infant monkey is raised with no real mother at all, what problems should you expect as it grows up?
items.back: It becomes anxious and insecure, and shows abnormal sexuality.
items.source_excerpt: Infant monkeys deprived of real mothers became anxious, insecure, show abnormal sexuality

items.front: What did Bowlby (1969) notice in human children, beyond Harlow's pattern?
items.back: Individual differences in children's behavior: some become anxious until mom returns (separation anxiety); others become depressed and show anger and detachment when mom returns.
items.source_excerpt: Bowlby (1969) noticed a similar pattern in humans • But, he also saw individual differences in kids’ behaviors

items.definition: A child's becoming anxious until the mother returns after being separated from her.
items.source_excerpt: Some become anxious until mom returns (separation anxiety)

items.definition: Ainsworth's procedure assessing how a child responds to being left with a friendly stranger for a few minutes and to the mother's return; it classifies children into three attachment styles.
items.source_excerpt: Ainsworth: Strange Situation Procedure – How does a child respond to being left with a friendly stranger for a few minutes?

items.definition: The attachment style of a child who continues exploring and playing when left and is happy to see mother on her return; in adults, finding it relatively easy to get close to and depend on others without worrying about abandonment.
items.source_excerpt: Continue exploration, play, happy to see mother upon return

items.definition: The attachment style of a child who is unfazed when mother leaves and avoidant upon her return; in adults, discomfort being close to others and difficulty trusting or depending on them.
items.source_excerpt: Unfazed when mother left, and avoidant upon return

items.definition: The attachment style of a child who is very anxious throughout the Strange Situation and clingy and angry on mother's return; in adults, wanting to get very close while worrying that the partner doesn't really love them.
items.source_excerpt: Very anxious throughout procedure, clingy and angry upon return

items.question: In Ainsworth's Strange Situation Procedure, a toddler barely reacts when mother leaves and turns away from her when she comes back. Which attachment style is this?
items.explanation: Being unfazed when mother leaves and avoidant upon return is the avoidant pattern.
distractor_rationale: Secure children are happy to see mother on her return.
Anxious-ambivalent children are very anxious throughout, then clingy and angry.
Separation anxiety means becoming anxious until mom returns — the reverse of being unfazed.
items.source_excerpt: 2. Unfazed when mother left, and avoidant upon return

items.question: A child is very distressed throughout the procedure and, when mother returns, clings to her while angrily pushing at her. Which style does this indicate?
items.explanation: Very anxious throughout, then clingy and angry on return, is the anxious-ambivalent pattern.
distractor_rationale: Avoidant children are unfazed and turn away on return.
Secure children keep playing and are happy to see mother return.
Separation anxiety (anxious until mom returns) lacks the angry clinging, and secure children are happy on return.
items.source_excerpt: 3. Very anxious throughout procedure, clingy and angry upon return

items.definition: Unconscious expectations, formed in early attachment, for how people will treat you in later relationships.
items.source_excerpt: “Internal working models” for later relationships • Unconscious expectations for how people will treat them

items.question: Which of these does a child's response in the Strange Situation NOT predict?
options: How responsive the mother is to the child's needs
The child's internal working models for relationships
items.explanation: The Strange Situation response predicts the mother's behavior toward the child, internal working models, and adult attachment styles — not psychosexual stages, which contemporary approaches cut.
distractor_rationale: Predicted — the mother's behavior, i.e., how responsive she is.
Predicted — unconscious expectations for how others will treat them.
Predicted — adult attachment styles.
items.source_excerpt: Child’s response in Strange Situation predicts: – Mother’s behavior toward child • How responsive to child’s needs?

items.front: What did Hazan and Shaver (1987) find?
items.back: Similar patterns of attachment in adult relationships: secure, avoidant, and anxious-ambivalent (preoccupied) relationship styles.
items.source_excerpt: Hazan and Shaver (1987) • Found similar patterns of attachment in adult relationships

items.question: An adult says: "Others are reluctant to get as close as I would like. I often worry my partner doesn't really love me, and wanting closeness sometimes scares people away." Which style is this?
items.explanation: Wanting to get very close and worrying about the partner's love is the anxious-ambivalent (preoccupied) self-description.
distractor_rationale: Avoidant adults are uncomfortable being close and nervous when anyone gets too close.
Secure adults don't worry about being abandoned.
Detachment describes pulling away, which fits avoidance — not someone seeking more closeness.
items.source_excerpt: I often worry that my partner doesn't really love me or won't want to stay with me.

items.question: Which self-description fits the avoidant adult style?
options: I find it easy to get close and to depend on others
I'm uneasy being close and find it hard to trust
I want very close bonds and worry I'll be abandoned
I worry my partner won't want to stay with me
items.explanation: The avoidant description: somewhat uncomfortable being close to others, finding it difficult to trust them completely or depend on them.
distractor_rationale: This is the secure description.
This is the anxious-ambivalent (preoccupied) description.
Also part of the anxious-ambivalent description.
items.source_excerpt: I am somewhat uncomfortable being close to others; I find it difficult to trust them completely, difficult to allow myself to depend on them.

items.question: Which finding about adult attachment styles is correct?
options: Preoccupied people have the most sex
Securely attached people have the least sex
items.explanation: Preoccupied people have the most sex and feel the greatest need for intimacy; avoidants have the least sex (except avoidant males) and worse memory for relationship concepts.
distractor_rationale: The preoccupied, not avoidants, feel the greatest need for intimacy.
Avoidants (except avoidant males), not secure people, have the least sex.
Worse memory for relationship concepts is found in avoidants.
items.source_excerpt: Preoccupied have most sex, Avoidant least (except for Avoidant males) – Preoccupied feel greatest need for intimacy

items.title: The stress test ('Machine') study
steps: Heterosexual romantic couples come to the lab; they're told the male must take part in an experiment involving 'the machine'.
The experimenter leaves the couple alone in a waiting room for 10 minutes, secretly videotaped.
The male participant feels stressed — how does the female participant respond?
Avoidant females were least likely to show support, if anything showing annoyance at their partner's nervousness.
Secure females were most supportive.
items.takeaway: Avoidantly attached people show discomfort with relationship-related emotions.
items.source_excerpt: Hetero romantic couples brought into lab; told that the male must participate in experiment involving the “machine”

items.question: In a waiting room, a man grows visibly nervous about an upcoming stressful experiment. Based on the stress-test study, which partner is most likely to respond with annoyance rather than support?
options: A partner with a preoccupied style
items.explanation: Avoidant females were least likely to show support and, if anything, showed annoyance at their partner's nervousness.
distractor_rationale: Secure females were the most supportive.
Preoccupied people seek intimacy; annoyance at a partner's need was the avoidant pattern.
Same style as anxious-ambivalent — not the one that showed annoyance.
items.source_excerpt: Avoidant females least likely to show support – If anything, show annoyance at partner’s nervousness

items.question: In a 2022 study, participants watched a 20-minute video of a woman describing her break-up (or a control video). What happened among anxiously attached participants?
options: They remembered fewer details, but only of the break-up video
They created false memories with extra details in both videos
They remembered both videos more accurately than avoidants
They created false memories, but only for the break-up video
items.explanation: Anxiously attached participants created false memories with additional details — in both conditions; avoidants failed to remember more details in the break-up condition.
distractor_rationale: This was the avoidants' result.
They added false details, so they weren't more accurate.
The false memories appeared in both conditions, not just the break-up one.
items.source_excerpt: In the break-up condition, avoidants failed to remember more details – Anxiously attached participants created false memories with additional details! • In both conditions!

items.question: A 37-year longitudinal study observed mothers with their babies, then about 35 years later measured the now-adults' physiological response to conflict with a romantic partner. What did it find?
options: No link between infancy and adult responses
Less sensitive mothers → smaller adult skin response
Less sensitive mothers → larger adult skin response
More sensitive mothers → larger adult skin response
items.explanation: Adults whose moms had shown less sensitivity had a larger skin conductance response to conflict with their partner — linking childhood and adult relationships.
distractor_rationale: The study is presented as showing a link.
Reverses the direction of the effect.
Pairs sensitive mothering with the stronger stress response — backwards.
items.source_excerpt: Adults whose moms had shown less sensitivity had larger skin conductance response to conflict with partner

items.question: Pooling 5 longitudinal studies from age 13 to 72 (Chopik, Edelstein & Grimm, 2017), how do anxious and avoidant attachment change with age?
options: Both rise steadily from adolescence into old age
Anxious declines after youth; avoidant stays steadier
Avoidant falls sharply with age while anxious stays stable
Neither style changes at all after adolescence
items.explanation: Anxious attachment is high in adolescence and young adulthood, then declines; avoidant attachment is more stable, with small declines across age.
distractor_rationale: Both decline rather than rise.
Swaps the two patterns.
Attachment styles can change across the lifespan — that is the study's point.
items.source_excerpt: Anxious attachment is high in adolescence and young adulthood, then declines • Avoidant attachment is more stable, small declines across age

items.front: Two 25-year-olds both have anxious attachment; one enters a long-term relationship and one stays single. Who is likelier to grow more secure over time?
items.back: The partnered one — being in a relationship fosters growing security over the years.
items.source_excerpt: Being in a relationship leads to greater 7 secure attachment over time

items.front: Why would knowing someone's attachment style help you forecast how they will act with a partner?
items.back: Because attachment style is a stable part of personality that forecasts conduct in close relationships.
items.source_excerpt: Important part of personality – Predict how people behave in relationships

sections.title: Lecture 4 — The Motives Approach: Murray, McClelland, McAdams
sections.description: What motives are and how they differ from Freud's instincts; Murray's needs, press and apperception; McClelland's implicit vs. self-attributed motives and the Big 3; McAdams on intimacy.

items.definition: Internal states that direct behavior, based on needs or tension; they can be conscious or unconscious.
items.source_excerpt: Internal states that direct behavior • Based on needs, or tension • Can be unconscious

items.question: Motives are similar to Freud's basic instincts. How do they differ?
options: Motives are always unconscious, like instincts
Broader range, and more emphasis on the ego
Motives are limited to sex and aggression
Motives play down awareness of one's needs
items.explanation: Compared with Freud's instincts, motives cover a broader range, can be conscious or unconscious, and place more emphasis on the ego (awareness of motives).
distractor_rationale: Motives can be conscious OR unconscious.
That narrow range describes Freud's instincts, not motives.
The reverse — motive theories put more emphasis on awareness of motives.
items.source_excerpt: Similar to Freud’s basic instincts but… – Broader range of motives – Can be conscious or unconscious – More emphasis on the ego (awareness of motives)

items.front: In what four ways are motives part of personality?
items.back: There are individual differences in the strength of various motives (e.g., achievement vs. affiliation); they contribute to major life outcomes (career success, marriage); they are stable over time; and they tell us (part of) why people behave the way they do.
items.source_excerpt: Individual differences in the strength of various motives – achievement vs. affiliation • Contribute to major life outcomes

items.front: Who are the 'three Ms' among the early motive theorists?
items.back: Murray, McClelland, and McAdams.
items.source_excerpt: 1. Early Motive Theorists – Murray, McClelland, McAdams

items.front: Where does Henry Murray sit in the history of motive theory, and how was he trained?
items.back: He offered the first modern motivation theory (1930s–60s); trained in medicine, he then studied psychoanalysis under Jung and became a 'reborn man'.
items.source_excerpt: First modern theory of motivation • Began as a medical doctor • Studied psychoanalysis with Jung

items.definition: In Murray's theory, a psychological force that guides behavior — a compulsion to reduce a state of tension.
items.source_excerpt: Need – Psychological force that guides behavior – Compulsion to reduce state of tension

items.definition: Murray's need for getting attention.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Needs According to Murray — Exhibition – Getting attention

items.definition: Murray's need for taking care of others.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Needs According to Murray — Nurturance – Taking care of others

items.definition: Murray's need: the desire to be taken care of.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Needs According to Murray — Succor – Desire to be taken care of

items.definition: Murray's need for lowering oneself.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Needs According to Murray — Abasement – Lowering oneself

items.front: A student constantly puts herself down and plays down her own worth in front of others. Which of Murray's needs is she showing?
items.back: Abasement — the need for lowering oneself.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Needs According to Murray — Abasement – Lowering oneself

items.definition: Murray's need to control others.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Needs According to Murray — Dominance – Control others

items.definition: Murray's need for independence.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Needs According to Murray — Autonomy – independence

items.question: A man constantly seeks out people who will look after him and handle his problems. Which of Murray's needs is strong in him?
items.explanation: Succor is the desire to be taken care of.
distractor_rationale: Nurturance is the reverse — taking care of others.
Order is another of Murray's needs; it has nothing to do with being cared for.
Affiliation/intimacy is closeness to others, not specifically being cared for.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Needs According to Murray — Nurturance – Taking care of others; Succor – Desire to be taken care of

items.question: A coworker always dresses to stand out and steers every meeting conversation back to herself. Which of Murray's needs fits best?
items.explanation: Exhibition is the need for getting attention.
distractor_rationale: Dominance is about controlling others, not being noticed.
Achievement is success seeking.
Autonomy is independence.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Needs According to Murray — Achievement – Success seeking; Exhibition – Getting attention

items.definition: Murray's term for the importance of the environment: needs are activated only in certain contexts.
items.source_excerpt: “Press” – Importance of environment – Needs are activated only in certain contexts

items.definition: Murray's term for the process through which we perceive the environment — a process influenced by our needs.
items.source_excerpt: “Apperception” – Process through which we perceive the environment – Influenced by needs

items.question: A student high in need for affiliation sees a crowded party as a chance to bond, while a classmate sees the same party as a threat. Which Murray concept explains the different perceptions?
items.explanation: Apperception is the process through which we perceive the environment, and it is influenced by our needs.
distractor_rationale: Press is about the environment activating needs in certain contexts, not needs shaping perception.
Succor is the need to be taken care of.
Another of Murray's needs, not a process of perceiving the environment.
items.source_excerpt: Process through which we perceive the environment – Influenced by needs

items.question: A woman's need for dominance shows up only in competitive workplace settings, never at home. Which of Murray's concepts does this illustrate?
items.explanation: Press captures the importance of the environment: needs are activated only in certain contexts.
distractor_rationale: Apperception is how needs shape perception of the environment, not context activating needs.
Exhibition is a need for attention, not a principle about context.
Order is one of Murray's needs, not a principle about when needs are activated.
items.source_excerpt: Needs are activated only in certain contexts

items.definition: In McClelland's theory, unconscious motives revealed by the TAT; unrelated to people's stated motives, they predict long-term outcomes such as career, marriage, health and stable beliefs.
items.source_excerpt: TAT reveals implicit (unconscious) motives – Implicit and explicit motives not related

items.definition: In McClelland's theory, the explicit motives people consciously report; they predict shorter-term behaviors and attitudes, such as performance on an experimental task.
items.source_excerpt: Explicit motives à Shorter term behaviors/attitudes • Performance on an experimental task

items.question: A researcher wants to predict who will have the most successful careers over the next 20 years. Which measure does McClelland's work suggest?
options: Explicit motives reported in a questionnaire
Implicit motives revealed by the TAT
Performance on a short lab task today
items.explanation: Implicit motives (revealed by the TAT) predict long-term outcomes like career success; explicit motives predict shorter-term behaviors.
distractor_rationale: Explicit motives predict shorter-term behaviors and attitudes.
Lab-task performance is what explicit motives predict, not long-term careers.
Self-attributed = explicit motives, which predict short-term behavior.
items.source_excerpt: Implicit motives à Long-term outcomes • Career, marriage, health, stable beliefs

items.question: Someone scores high on a self-report achievement scale. What can we infer about their implicit achievement motive?
options: It must be low, by compensation
It will match after one week
items.explanation: McClelland found implicit and explicit motives are not related, so the self-report tells us nothing about the implicit motive.
distractor_rationale: Assumes the two kinds of motive are correlated, which they are not.
There's no inverse relation either — they are simply unrelated.
Invents a convergence over time; the two are not related.
items.source_excerpt: Implicit and explicit motives not related

items.front: Which three motives did McClelland treat as central to personality?
items.back: Achievement, power, and affiliation (with intimacy).
items.source_excerpt: Big 3 Motives – Achievement – Power – Affiliation (and Intimacy)

items.definition: A motive marked by preferring moderate levels of challenge (it must feel tough, but still allow success), desiring performance feedback, and choosing careers with some risk and much personal responsibility.
items.source_excerpt: Preference for moderate levels of challenge – Need to feel it’s tough, but still succeed • Desire for performance feedback

items.question: A person high in the achievement motive can choose a puzzle to work on. Which will they most likely pick?
options: The easiest puzzle, to guarantee success
A moderately hard one they can still solve
The hardest puzzle, almost surely unsolvable
Any puzzle, as long as no one gives feedback
items.explanation: Achievement-motivated people prefer moderate challenge: it needs to feel tough, but they must still succeed. They also want performance feedback.
distractor_rationale: Too easy — it wouldn't feel tough.
Too hard — they need to still succeed.
They desire performance feedback, not avoid it.
items.source_excerpt: Preference for moderate levels of challenge – Need to feel it’s tough, but still succeed

items.definition: A motive marked by seeking control over others, being argumentative and risk-taking, and preferring less popular friends so as to have the most power.
items.source_excerpt: Seek control over others • Argumentative • Risk-taking • Prefer less popular friends

items.question: Why does someone high in the power motive tend to choose less popular friends?
options: They need to have the most power
They fear rejection by popular people
They value a few very close bonds
items.explanation: Power-motivated people prefer less popular friends because they need to have the most power in the group.
distractor_rationale: Nurturing others is a different need (nurturance).
Fear of rejection isn't part of the power motive's description.
A few very close friends describes the intimacy motive (McAdams).
items.source_excerpt: Prefer less popular friends – Need to have the most power

items.definition: A motive focused most on relationships and related to happiness and satisfaction with life; McAdams argued it matters more than affiliation — people high in it have a few very close friends rather than many acquaintances.
items.source_excerpt: Dan McAdams: argued that intimacy is more important than affiliation

items.question: According to Dan McAdams, how would a person high in the intimacy motive structure their social life?
options: A large network of casual acquaintances
items.explanation: People high in the intimacy motive have a few very close friends rather than a large number of acquaintances.
distractor_rationale: The reverse of McAdams's claim — breadth rather than depth.
Choosing less popular friends is the power motive.
Independence is Murray's need for autonomy.
items.source_excerpt: People high in this motive have a few very close friends, rather than a large number of acquaintances

items.question: An employee picks a job with real risk and lots of personal responsibility, and keeps asking her manager how well she's doing. Which motive is she high in?
items.explanation: Desire for performance feedback and choosing careers with some risk and much personal responsibility mark the achievement motive.
distractor_rationale: Power involves seeking control over others; risk-taking overlaps, but feedback-seeking doesn't.
Intimacy focuses on close relationships.
One of Murray's needs; avoiding blame clashes with seeking personal responsibility.
items.source_excerpt: Desire for performance feedback • Choose careers with some risk and much personal responsibility

sections.title: Lecture 4 — The Humanistic (Phenomenological) Perspective: Maslow and Rogers
sections.description: Basic assumptions of the humanistic perspective, Maslow's hierarchy of needs and self-actualization, critiques and the evolutionary revision of the pyramid, and Rogers's client-centered therapy.

items.definition: A more clinical than research-based approach that applies motive theory to help people make their lives better, focusing on subjective experience, conscious motives and awareness of needs, and individuals taking responsibility for their own life outcomes.
items.source_excerpt: More clinical than research based; attempt to take motive theory and apply it help people make their lives better

items.definition: Subjective experience — the focus of the humanistic perspective, which holds that individuals differ in their perception of reality and that subjective reality matters more than objective reality.
items.source_excerpt: Focused on phenomenology, or subjective experience

items.question: Two siblings grew up in the same house; one remembers it as warm, the other as cold. To a humanistic psychologist, which account matters most for understanding each sibling?
options: The objective facts about the house
Each sibling's own perception of it
The parents' account of the house
items.explanation: The humanistic perspective emphasizes phenomenology: individual differences in the perception of reality, with subjective reality more important than objective reality.
distractor_rationale: Objective reality is considered less important than subjective reality.
An outside observer's view isn't the person's subjective experience.
Accuracy is about objective reality, which this view ranks below subjective reality.
items.source_excerpt: Individual differences in the perception of reality – Subjective reality is more important than objective reality

items.front: What are the three basic assumptions of the humanistic perspective?
items.back: 1. Emphasis on phenomenology (subjective reality matters more than objective reality). 2. Self-actualization (people are intrinsically good and strive toward health, maturity and autonomy — growth-based, not need-based). 3. Emphasis on self/identity (a universal need for positive self-regard).
items.source_excerpt: Self-Actualization – People are intrinsically good and strive toward greater health, maturity, and autonomy – Growth based rather than need based

items.question: How does the humanistic perspective's view of human motivation contrast with earlier motive theories?
options: It sees people as driven only by tension reduction
It sees striving as growth-based, not need-based
It sees human nature as basically destructive
It sees motives as mostly unconscious drives
items.explanation: Humanistic theorists see people as intrinsically good and striving toward health, maturity and autonomy — growth-based rather than need-based — with a focus on conscious motives.
distractor_rationale: Tension reduction is Murray's definition of a need — the need-based view.
That is Freud's death instinct view; humanists see people as intrinsically good.
Humanists put greater focus on conscious motives and awareness of needs.
items.source_excerpt: People are intrinsically good and strive toward greater health, maturity, and autonomy – Growth based rather than need based

items.definition: Maslow's top need: the desire for fulfillment — the tendency to become actually what one is potentially, everything one is capable of becoming; it brings enriched experiences, enhanced creativity, and being in touch with (not threatened by) feelings.
items.source_excerpt: It refers to man's desire for fulfillment, namely to the tendency for him to become actually in what he is potentially

items.definition: Maslow's theory, based on his clinical practice, that human needs are ordered from physiological, safety, belongingness and love, and esteem up to self-actualization, with needs at the basic level met first.
items.source_excerpt: Developed a theory of human needs, based on his clinical practice

items.definition: In Maslow's hierarchy, the principle that needs at the basic level are met first; physiological needs are the most prepotent.
items.source_excerpt: Prepotency of needs: Needs at basic level met first

items.question: A refugee has gone two days without food and is sleeping outdoors in danger. According to Maslow's prepotency principle, which need will dominate their attention?
items.explanation: Needs at the basic level are met first, and physiological needs (food, water, air, sleep) are the most prepotent — they come before safety.
distractor_rationale: A higher level that waits until physiological and safety needs are met.
A higher level still.
Pressing too, but safety sits above physiological needs in prepotency.
items.source_excerpt: Needs for food, water, air, sleep, sex – Most “prepotent”

items.question: In Maslow's hierarchy, which level sits directly above safety needs?
options: Esteem needs from self and others
items.explanation: From the bottom: physiological, safety, belongingness and love, esteem, self-actualization (with peak experiences at the apex).
distractor_rationale: Esteem sits one level higher, above belongingness and love.
Physiological needs are below safety, at the base.
Self-actualization is at the top, above esteem.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs — Peak experiences; Need for Self-Actualization (creative); Esteem Needs (confident, worthy); Belongingness and Love Needs (warmth); Safety Needs (security); Physiological Needs (hunger)

items.definition: The base of Maslow's hierarchy: needs for food, water, air, sleep and sex — the most prepotent; civilization's function is to satisfy them so we can focus on higher needs.
items.source_excerpt: Needs for food, water, air, sleep, sex

items.definition: Maslow's second level: shelter, security, freedom from threat or danger, and order, structure and predictability — e.g., having a place to live and being able to pay bills.
items.source_excerpt: Shelter, security, freedom from threat or danger • Order, structure, predictability

items.definition: Maslow's third level: needs for affiliation, family, group identity, intimate relationships and relatedness — the need both to receive and to give love.
items.source_excerpt: Needs for affiliation, family, group identity, intimate relationships, relatedness • Need to receive and to give love

items.definition: Maslow's fourth level: the need to be held in high regard by self and others (not just 'self-esteem'), coming from mastery, achievement, adequacy, competence, confidence and independence.
items.source_excerpt: Need to be held in high regard by self and others (not just “self-esteem”)

items.question: A student says Maslow's esteem needs are just about feeling good about yourself. What does this miss?
options: They are mainly about receiving love
They include high regard from others
They include the need for security
items.explanation: Esteem needs are the need to be held in high regard by self AND others — not just 'self-esteem'.
distractor_rationale: Receiving and giving love is the belongingness and love level.
Security belongs to safety needs.
Creativity is linked to self-actualization.
items.source_excerpt: Need to be held in high regard by self and others (not just “self-esteem”)

items.question: After a layoff, a man's main worry is whether he can keep paying rent and bills. Which of Maslow's needs is threatened?
items.explanation: Having a place to live and being able to pay bills are safety needs (shelter, security, predictability).
distractor_rationale: Losing a job could hurt regard, but rent and bills are about security.
Belongingness concerns affiliation and love.
Physiological needs are food, water, air, sleep and sex.
items.source_excerpt: Having a place to live, ability to pay bills, etc.

items.definition: Experiences at the apex of Maslow's hierarchy in which time and place are transcended and one feels unity of self with the universe and a feeling of power and wonder; they manifest differently for each person and are common in psychologically healthy people.
items.source_excerpt: Time and place are transcended – Experience unity of self with universe – Feeling of power and wonder

items.question: Which set of characteristics describes a self-actualized person?
options: Conformity, constant company, rare peak experiences
items.explanation: Self-actualized people show self-acceptance, solitude, independence from culture, frequent peak experiences and creativity.
distractor_rationale: The opposite of independence from culture, solitude and frequent peak experiences.
The opposite of self-acceptance and independence.
These describe narcissism, not self-actualization.
items.source_excerpt: Self-acceptance • Solitude • Independence from culture • Frequent peak experiences • Creativity

items.front: Complete Maslow: "A musician must make music, an artist must paint, a poet must write… What a man can be, …"
items.back: "…he must be. This is the need we may call self-actualization."
items.source_excerpt: What a man can be, he must be. This is the need we may call self-actualization

items.front: In Maslow's view, why does a society that reliably feeds and shelters people free them for personal growth?
items.back: Civilization's job is to satisfy basic physiological needs so that people can turn to higher ones.
items.source_excerpt: Function of civilization, society is to satisfy these needs so we can focus on the higher ones

items.question: Critics call Maslow's hierarchy 'aspirational but not normative.' What does this mean?
options: It describes what people actually do
It applies only to clinical patients
It is supported by evolutionary theory
items.explanation: Aspirational but not normative: it says what people 'should' do, not what they actually do.
distractor_rationale: That would be normative — the very thing the critique says it isn't.
Though based on clinical practice, the critique isn't about who it applies to.
The second critique is that it is inconsistent with evolutionary understanding.
items.source_excerpt: Aspirational but not normative – What people ‘should’ do, not what they do do

items.question: Why is Maslow's placement of creativity at the top seen as inconsistent with evolutionary theory?
options: Creativity is a low-level means to reproductive ends
Creativity is the most prepotent of all human needs
Evolution treats creativity as purely self-fulfilling
Creativity is unrelated to survival or reproduction
items.explanation: According to evolutionary theory, creativity is a lower-level means to more ultimate reproductive ends — so self-fulfillment through creativity doesn't explain how it helps the species survive.
distractor_rationale: Physiological needs are the most prepotent, not creativity.
Self-fulfillment is Maslow's account, which the critique rejects.
Evolutionary theory ties creativity to reproductive ends.
items.source_excerpt: According to evolutionary theory, creativity is a lower level means to more ultimate reproductive ends

items.question: In Kenrick, Griskevicius, Neuberg & Schaller's (2010) evolutionary revision of Maslow's pyramid, what sits at the top in place of self-actualization?
items.explanation: The revised pyramid runs immediate physiological needs, self-protection, affiliation, status/esteem, mate acquisition, mate retention, and parenting at the top — 'self-actualization has been dethroned'.
distractor_rationale: Mate retention is just below parenting.
Status/esteem is in the middle, below the mating levels.
Mate acquisition sits below mate retention.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Parenting; Mate Retention; Mate Acquisition; Status/Esteem; Affiliation; Self-Protection; Immediate Physiological Needs (Kenrick, Griskevicius, Neuberg, & Schaller, 2010)
