items.alt_text: Two pyramids side by side. Left, Maslow's hierarchy from bottom to top: physiological needs (hunger), safety (security), belongingness and love, esteem, self-actualization, with peak experiences at the apex. Right, Kenrick and colleagues' 2010 revision from bottom to top: immediate physiological needs, self-protection, affiliation, status/esteem, mate acquisition, mate retention, and parenting at the top.
items.caption: Both pyramids start with physiological needs and keep affiliation and esteem in the middle; the revision replaces self-actualization with mating and parenting goals.
items.source_excerpt: Let’s make a hierarchy based on evolutionarily derived and empirically supported needs

items.front: What did Maslow get right, and what lacks evidence, according to the modern evolutionary take?
items.back: Right: shedding light on psychological (not just physical) needs. No evidence: some aspects of the hierarchy — e.g., whether people intrinsically/innately strive for self-actualization.
items.source_excerpt: Maslow was right to shed light on psychological (not just physical) needs

items.front: Why was the evolutionary revision of Maslow's pyramid highly controversial?
items.back: 'Self-actualization has been dethroned' — it drew anger from the childless (is parenting too glorified?) and from the humanities (why do evolutionary scientists always put mating above the arts?).
items.source_excerpt: Anger from the childless – Is parenting too glorified? • Anger from the humanities

items.front: What did Carl Rogers believe about human nature and how goodness develops?
items.back: People are intrinsically good and strive toward self-understanding, self-acceptance, maturity and autonomy; they can develop their innate goodness if society acts in helpful, encouraging and affirming ways.
items.source_excerpt: People can develop innate goodness if society acts in helpful, encouraging, and affirming ways

items.definition: Rogers's route to becoming 'fully functioning': a trusting, accepting, empathetic therapist shows unconditional positive regard so the client can express and accept their authentic self.
items.source_excerpt: “Client-centered therapy” – Therapist is trusting, accepting, empathetic

items.definition: Love and acceptance, regardless of what the person does — shown by the therapist in client-centered therapy.
items.source_excerpt: Therapist shows unconditional positive regard for client • Love and acceptance, regardless of what the person does

items.definition: Being able to express and accept one's authentic self — the goal of client-centered therapy and a characteristic of the self-actualized person.
items.source_excerpt: Client able to express and accept his/her authentic self (self-acceptance)

items.question: A client confesses something they're deeply ashamed of. How would a therapist practicing client-centered therapy respond?
options: Point out the behavior was wrong and set conditions
Accept the client warmly, regardless of the act
Probe for the repressed childhood memory behind it
Interpret the confession as an id impulse
items.explanation: Client-centered therapists show unconditional positive regard — love and acceptance regardless of what the person does — so the client can accept their authentic self.
distractor_rationale: Setting conditions is the opposite of unconditional positive regard.
Uncovering repressed memories is a psychoanalytic approach.
Interpreting id impulses is Freudian, not Rogerian.
items.source_excerpt: Love and acceptance, regardless of what the person does

items.question: Maslow and Rogers both saw people as intrinsically good. Which idea is specifically Rogers's?
options: Needs at the basic level are met first
Goodness grows if society is affirming
Civilization exists to meet basic needs
items.explanation: Rogers held that people can develop innate goodness if society acts in helpful, encouraging and affirming ways.
distractor_rationale: Prepotency is Maslow's principle.
Peak experiences are part of Maslow's hierarchy.
Maslow's view of the function of civilization.
items.source_excerpt: People can develop innate goodness if society acts in helpful, encouraging, and affirming ways

sections.title: Lecture 4 — The Self
sections.description: The 'I' and the 'Me', self-consciousness vs. self-concept, assessing the self-concept, how we know a child (or animal) has a self, the looking-glass self, and whether multiple selves are adaptive.

items.front: In Susan Harter's mirror illustration, what are the two aspects of the self?
items.back: The 'I' — the active observer — and the 'Me' in the mirror — the Me as observed.
items.source_excerpt: There is the I, the active observer, and there is the Me in the mirror, the Me as observed.

items.definition: William James's 'I': the self as agent doing the observing — the self as perceiver; self-awareness.
items.source_excerpt: Self-consciousness – The “I” – Self-awareness

items.definition: William James's 'Me': the self as an object that can be observed ('I have property X') — one's conception of oneself as a physical, social, psychological and moral being.
items.source_excerpt: Self-concept – The “Me” – Conception of one’s self as a physical, social, psychological, moral being

items.question: In the middle of a presentation, you suddenly notice yourself blushing. In William James's terms, which part of the self is doing the noticing?
options: The 'Me' — the self as an object
items.explanation: The 'I' is the self as agent doing the observing (self-consciousness); the blushing self being noticed is the 'Me'.
distractor_rationale: The 'Me' is what is being noticed — the blushing self as observed.
The self-concept is the 'Me', not the observer.
Self-liking is an evaluation, not the act of observing.
items.source_excerpt: The “I” • Self as agent doing the observing • Self as the perceiver

items.question: "I am a good tennis player" is a statement about which aspect of the self?
items.explanation: Statements of the form 'I have property X' describe the 'Me' — the self as object, i.e., the self-concept.
distractor_rationale: The 'I' is the observer, not the property being described.
Self-consciousness is the 'I' — self-awareness.
The perceiver is the 'I'.
items.source_excerpt: Self as object that can be observed • “I have property X

items.front: What is the relationship between self-schemas and the overall self-concept?
items.back: Schemas are its building blocks: many of them join together and interact to produce the overall picture of who you are.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Self-Schemas — “Self-schemas combine and interact to form our self-concept.”

items.question: In a hierarchical model of the self-concept, under which branch does a person's view of their physical appearance fall?
items.explanation: The general self-concept splits into nonacademic and academic (English, Math) branches; physical ability, physical appearance and relationships sit under the nonacademic branch.
distractor_rationale: The math branch covers mathematics and school-related views.
The English branch covers reading and school-related views.
General school is a lower-level academic facet, not where appearance belongs.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Sample Self-Concept Structure — General Self-concept; Nonacademic Self-concept; Academic English Self-concept; Academic Math Self-concept; Physical Ability; Physical Appearance

items.definition: A way of assessing the self-concept in which a person, imagining they want someone to know what they are really like, completes 'I am ____' twenty times; answers are then classified into categories.
items.source_excerpt: Imagine that you want someone to know what you are really like. You can tell this person 20 things about yourself

items.question: On the Twenty Statements task, a student writes "I am 19 years old" and "I am someone's daughter." How are these classified?
items.explanation: Age, race, ethnicity and being a daughter are ascribed identities.
distractor_rationale: Social/group identities are affiliations like 'student' or 'Democrat'.
Personal characteristics are traits like friendly, happy, ambitious.
Interests/activities are things like painter, stamp collector or jazz fan.
items.source_excerpt: Ascribed Identities (age, race, ethnicity, daughter)

items.question: "I am a member of the debate team" would be classified in which Twenty Statements category?
items.explanation: Membership in a group, like 'student' or 'Democrat', is a social and group identity.
distractor_rationale: Interests/activities are things like painter or jazz fan — a hobby, not membership.
Material possessions are things owned, like a VW.
Ascribed identities are given, like age or ethnicity, not joined.
items.source_excerpt: Social and Group Identities (student, Democrat) • Interests/Activities (painter, stamp collector, jazz fan)

items.front: What are the six categories used to classify Twenty Statements answers?
items.back: Personal characteristics; ascribed identities; social and group identities; interests/activities; material possessions; abstract/existential.
items.source_excerpt: Personal Characteristics (friendly, happy, ambitious) • Ascribed Identities (age, race, ethnicity, daughter)

items.question: Which marker of a child's sense of self typically appears LAST?
items.explanation: Linguistic markers appear around 18 months, cognitive-behavioral markers at 18–24 months, and emotional markers (self-conscious emotions, empathy) at 2.5–3 years.
distractor_rationale: Linguistic markers appear around 18 months — the earliest.
A cognitive-behavioral marker at 18–24 months.
Also a cognitive-behavioral marker at 18–24 months.
items.source_excerpt: Emotional markers (age 2.5-3) – Self-conscious emotions • Shame • Guilt • Embarrassment • Pride

items.question: An 18-month-old starts saying "Mine!" and telling short stories about things that happened to her. Which kind of self marker is this?
items.explanation: Self-referencing ('I', 'me', 'mine') and narrative language about personally significant events are linguistic markers (age 18 months).
distractor_rationale: Cognitive-behavioral markers are imitation, role-taking and mirror self-recognition.
Emotional markers are self-conscious emotions and empathy at 2.5–3.
Mirror self-recognition is a cognitive-behavioral marker, not about language.
items.source_excerpt: Linguistic markers (age 18 months) – Self-referencing (“I” “Me” “Mine”) – Narrative language use

items.front: A 20-month-old recognizes herself in a mirror. Which category of self marker is that, and what else falls in the same category?
items.back: Cognitive-behavioral (about 18–24 months), together with imitation and role-taking and the rouge test.
items.source_excerpt: Cognitive-behavioral markers (18-24 months) – Imitation and role-taking – Mirror self-recognition – Rouge test

items.question: Which of these animals does NOT show mirror self-recognition?
items.explanation: Chimps, orangutans and gorillas show mirror self-recognition, but not monkeys; elephants, dolphins, humans, crows and magpies do.
distractor_rationale: Magpies, like crows, do show mirror self-recognition.
Dolphins show it.
Elephants show it.
items.source_excerpt: Chimps, orangutans, gorillas • But not monkeys – Elephants – Dolphins – Humans – Crows – Magpies

items.definition: Shame, guilt, embarrassment and pride — emotions that require the ability to evaluate the self (the 'I' evaluating the 'Me'); promoted by Freud's superego and emerging around age 2.5–3.
items.source_excerpt: Require ability to evaluate the self (“I” self evaluates the “me” self)

items.question: Why can't a 12-month-old feel genuine guilt, embarrassment or pride?
options: They need the 'I' to evaluate the 'Me'
These emotions require the ability to talk
These emotions develop only after puberty
These emotions come only from the id
items.explanation: Self-conscious emotions require the ability to evaluate the self — the 'I' evaluating the 'Me' — which emerges around 2.5–3 years.
distractor_rationale: Language markers appear at 18 months, but the requirement is self-evaluation, not speech.
They emerge at 2.5–3 years, long before puberty.
In Freud's model the superego, not the id, promotes them.
items.source_excerpt: Emotional markers (age 2.5-3) – Self-conscious emotions

items.definition: Charles Cooley's idea that the self is socially constructed: our sense of self is built on the life-long experience of seeing ourselves through the eyes of others.
items.source_excerpt: Our sense of self is built upon the life-long experience of seeing ourselves through the eyes of others

items.question: A teenager comes to see herself as funny mainly because friends always laugh at her jokes. Which idea does this illustrate?
items.explanation: Building a sense of self from seeing yourself through others' eyes is Cooley's looking glass self — the self is socially constructed.
distractor_rationale: The collective unconscious holds ancestral images shared by all humanity.
Prepotency is about meeting basic needs first.
Apperception is how needs shape our perception of the environment.
items.source_excerpt: Self is socially constructed • Our sense of self is built upon the life-long experience of seeing ourselves through the eyes of others

items.front: In one week (before social media), how many people and interactions did a typical university student have — and why does it matter for the looking glass self?
items.back: About 50 different people and 146 different interactions — many different 'mirrors', raising the question of whether we have a different self for each.
items.source_excerpt: the typical university student interacted with 50 different people and had 146 different interactions

items.definition: Seeing oneself very differently across one's social roles (child, friend, student, partner, worker); a highly differentiated self-concept.
items.source_excerpt: Multiple selves correspond to multiple roles--we see ourselves differently in each social role

items.definition: Seeing oneself similarly across one's different social roles — the comparison group to multiple selves.
items.source_excerpt: Compared people who saw themselves similarly across social roles (unitary selves)

items.question: Compared with people who see themselves similarly across their roles, what did the study find for people with highly 'multiple' selves?
options: Higher well-being, since they adapt to each role
Lower well-being and self-esteem, then and later
No difference in well-being or self-esteem
Lower self-esteem in university, gone by mid-life
items.explanation: Compared with people who have a unitary self, those with multiple selves had lower well-being and self-esteem during university and again 20 years later at mid-life.
distractor_rationale: The intuitive 'flexibility' answer, contradicted by the findings.
Differences were found in both well-being and self-esteem.
The link persisted 20 years later at mid-life.
items.source_excerpt: Multiple selves à lower well-being and self-esteem • During university years • 20 years later during mid-life

items.question: Which of these predicted having multiple selves 20 years later?
options: A stable career and long-lasting relationships
Low well-being and self-esteem in university
Strong mirror self-recognition as a child
items.explanation: Low well-being and self-esteem in university predicted multiple selves 20 years later, as did frequent relationship and career changes.
distractor_rationale: The reverse of the finding.
Frequent relationship and career changes — the opposite — predicted multiple selves.
Childhood self-recognition wasn't part of this study.
items.source_excerpt: Low well-being and self-esteem in universityà multiple selves 20 years later – Frequent relationship and career changes à multiple selves

items.front: A friend says having a totally different self for each relationship shows healthy flexibility. What did research conclude instead?
items.back: That a highly differentiated self-concept signals fragmentation — the absence of an integrated core self.
items.source_excerpt: A highly differentiated selfconcept reflects psychological fragmentation and lack of an integrated core self

items.title: Is it adaptive to have multiple selves?
steps: Compare people who see themselves similarly across social roles (unitary selves) with those who see themselves very differently (multiple selves).
Assessment: rate yourself on traits (assertive, try to be helpful, punctual, worry a lot, clever/witty) separately as son/daughter, friend, student, partner and worker.
Finding: multiple selves → lower well-being and self-esteem, during university and 20 years later at mid-life.
Finding: low well-being and self-esteem in university → multiple selves 20 years later; frequent relationship and career changes → multiple selves.
Conclusion: a highly differentiated self-concept reflects fragmentation and the lack of an integrated core self.
items.takeaway: Presenting a very different self in each role is not a sign of healthy flexibility.
items.source_excerpt: Study: Compared people who saw themselves similarly across social roles (unitary selves) with those who saw themselves very differently across their social roles (multiple selves)

sections.title: Lecture 4 — Self-Esteem
sections.description: Defining and measuring self-esteem (Rosenberg scale), how it changes across university, and its trajectory from age 9 to 90 in a large cross-sectional internet study.

items.definition: A global evaluation (positive vs. negative) of one's self as a physical, social, psychological and moral being, with an affective component (feelings about the self; self-liking) and a cognitive component (thoughts about one's competencies and abilities).
items.source_excerpt: Evaluation (positive vs. negative) of one’s self as a physical, social, psychological, and moral being

items.question: "I'm good at figuring out hard problems" reflects which component of self-esteem?
items.explanation: The cognitive component is thoughts about one's competencies and abilities; the affective component is feelings about the self (self-liking).
distractor_rationale: The affective component is feelings about the self — self-liking — not judgments of ability.
It's an evaluation of competence, which is part of self-esteem's cognitive component.
Not a component of self-esteem; the looking glass self concerns where the self-concept comes from.
items.source_excerpt: Affective component • Feelings about the self; self-liking – Cognitive component • Thoughts about one’s competencies, abilities

items.question: Which statement expresses self-esteem rather than self-concept?
options: "I am a psychology student and a Democrat."
"On the whole, I am satisfied with myself."
"I am a jazz fan and a stamp collector."
items.explanation: Self-esteem is a global positive-vs-negative evaluation of the self; the other statements describe the 'Me' without evaluating it.
distractor_rationale: Social/group identities — descriptions in the self-concept, not evaluations.
Ascribed identities and a personal fact — part of the self-concept.
Interests/activities — self-concept descriptions, not an evaluation.
items.source_excerpt: Self-esteem – Global evaluation (positive vs. negative) of one’s self

items.front: What are four ways of measuring self-esteem?
items.back: Self-report scales; similarity between actual and ideal self; observer report (e.g., parent and teacher ratings for kids); pictorial measures for children.
items.source_excerpt: Self-report scales • Similarity between actual and ideal self • Observer report

items.question: A researcher wants to measure a 5-year-old's self-esteem but the child can't read a questionnaire. Which approach is suggested for young children?
options: A pictorial measure, or parent and teacher ratings
The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, read silently
A single online item such as 'I have high self-esteem'
items.explanation: For children, self-esteem can be measured with pictorial measures or observer reports from parents and teachers.
distractor_rationale: A self-report scale for readers; the child can't complete it.
The cross-sectional study's item was still a written self-report.
The TIPI measures five personality dimensions, not self-esteem.
items.source_excerpt: Parent and teacher ratings for kids – Can someone else know your self-esteem? • Pictorial measures for children

items.definition: A 10-item self-report measure of self-esteem rated from strongly disagree (1) to strongly agree (5), with five negatively worded items (e.g., 'At times I think I am no good at all') reverse-scored.
items.source_excerpt: Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale

items.question: Which Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale item is reverse-scored?
options: I feel that I have a number of good qualities
I take a positive attitude toward myself
I wish I could have more respect for myself
I am able to do things as well as most other people
items.explanation: Negatively worded items like 'I wish I could have more respect for myself' are marked (R) and reverse-scored, so agreeing lowers the self-esteem score.
distractor_rationale: Positively worded — agreement directly indicates higher self-esteem.
Positively worded — scored as is.
Positively worded — scored as is.
items.source_excerpt: I wish I could have more respect for myself. (R)

items.front: An undergraduate scores 3.2 on the Rosenberg scale (1–5). Is that above or below the typical undergraduate?
items.back: Below — the undergraduate mean is 3.85 (from 1,643 psychology students).
items.source_excerpt: Undergraduates’ mean self-esteem • 3.85 • Based on 1,643 psych students

items.question: A longitudinal study tracked undergraduates' self-esteem from the start of Year 1 through the end of Year 4. When was self-esteem lowest?
options: At the very beginning of Year 1
At the end of first semester
items.explanation: Self-esteem dropped sharply by the end of the first semester, then recovered and rose over the following years.
distractor_rationale: Self-esteem fell after this starting point.
By Year 2 it had recovered above its starting level.
By Year 4 it was at its highest.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: SELF-ESTEEM CHANGE DURING UNIVERSITY — Week 1, Sem. 1, Year 1, Year 2, Year 3, Year 4; “End of 1st semester”

items.title: Self-esteem across university: a longitudinal study
steps: Undergraduates completed the Rosenberg scale at (1) the beginning of Year 1, (2) the end of first semester, and (3) the end of Years 1, 2, 3 and 4.
Self-esteem plunged at the end of the first semester.
It then rebounded by the end of Year 1 and kept rising through Year 4.
A student whose self-esteem fell: 'College shattered that bubble… There are so many people here who are much better than I am.'
A student whose self-esteem rose: 'I am proud of my work and what I accomplish.'
items.takeaway: The first semester is a low point; for most students self-esteem recovers and grows over university.
items.source_excerpt: Assessed undergrads’ self-esteem – Used Rosenberg scale (1) Beginning of Year 1 (2) End of first semester

items.front: What reason did a student whose self-esteem dropped give in the university longitudinal study?
items.back: They had thought they were one of the best students in school, but college 'shattered that bubble' — there were so many people who were much better (and their GPA felt like a verdict on them).
items.source_excerpt: I used to think I was the best or one of the best students in school. College shattered that bubble

items.front: How was self-esteem measured in the cross-sectional internet study, and how many people took part?
items.back: With one item — agree vs. disagree with 'I have high self-esteem' — in an online questionnaire that gave personality feedback; 127,838 people aged 9 to 90.
items.source_excerpt: Self-Esteem assessed with item: – Rate the extent to which you agree vs. disagree with this statement: “I have high self-esteem”

items.question: In the cross-sectional study of 127,838 people aged 9 to 90, what was the overall shape of self-esteem across the lifespan?
options: Steady rise from childhood all the way into old age
Drops in adolescence, climbs to the 60s, then falls
Low in childhood, peaks in adolescence, then declines
Flat across all ages, with no clear rise or fall
items.explanation: Self-esteem was high at 9–12, dropped in adolescence (13–17) and stayed low into the early 20s, rose gradually through adulthood to a peak around 61–70, then fell sharply at 71–80.
distractor_rationale: Misses both the adolescent drop and the late-life decline.
Reverses the adolescent pattern — adolescence is a low point, not a peak.
The trajectory shows clear rises and falls.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Trajectory of Self-Esteem from Age 9 to 90 — 9 to 12, 13 to 17, 18 to 23, 24 to 30, 31 to 40, 41 to 50, 51 to 60, 61 to 70, 71 to 80

items.question: Between which two pairs of adjacent age groups did self-esteem drop most steeply?
items.explanation: The two sharp falls are entering adolescence (9–12 to 13–17) and late life (61–70 to 71–80).
distractor_rationale: Self-esteem was flat or rising across these transitions.
These are near-flat stretches of the curve.
These are periods of gradual rise, especially into the 60s.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: Trajectory of Self-Esteem from Age 9 to 90 — 9 to 12, 13 to 17, 61 to 70, 71 to 80

items.front: How did the self-esteem trajectory of people living within the U.S. compare with those living outside it?
items.back: Both followed the same overall pattern — high in childhood, a drop in adolescence, then a rise across adulthood — with U.S. residents generally scoring somewhat higher at most ages.
items.source_excerpt: Figure: U.S. vs. Other countries — Living within U.S., Living outside U.S; Self-Esteem by Age
